As St. Paul says: “To the end he may stablish your hearts unblameable in holiness before God, even our Father, at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ with all his saints” (1 Thess 3:13), “Follow peace with all men, and holiness, without which no man shall see the Lord” (Heb 12:14).
He also calls them to listen to the counsel he offers them that they may be disciplined, that is, accept the Lord’s discipline with joy so as to bear the image of the Holy One.
* He who dreams that he is able to enter heaven without purity of heart and righteousness of life and holiness of body dies in this illusion, to awake and find himself in eternal shame and disgrace.

entries.section: 1. A final warning to the leaders

paragraphs.text: St. Irenaeus: Therefore desire my words, and long for them, that you may be instructed. [11]

As the wise man speaks in a spirit of love, in true longing for their growth and success, he asks them in a spirit of sincere brotherhood to desire his words, and to yearn for them or long for them, so that they may have true knowledge or fitting teachings.

He does not ask them for obedience, as one who commands so that they are bound to submit and carry out. Rather, in a spirit of love he guides and reveals the secrets of the successful life and of the way that leads them to eternal glories; therefore he begs them to review the matter, that their hearts may be kindled with longing toward the truth.

entries.section: 2. Wisdom comes to meet man

paragraphs.text: 13 For wisdom is bright and does not fade, and the beholding of her is easy for those who love her, and the finding of her is easy for those who seek her. 14 For she goes before and shows herself to those who desire her, 15 and whoever is early in seeking her does not labor, for he finds her sitting at his doors. 16 For meditation upon her is the perfection of prudence, and whoever watches for her sake will not long have care. 17 For she goes about seeking those who are worthy of her, and appears to them in the ways smiling, and meets them whenever they meditate upon her. 18 For the beginning of her is sincerity in the desire for discipline. 19 And the seeking of discipline is love, and love is the keeping of the laws, and the observing of the laws is the steadfastness of purity. 20 And purity brings near to God. 21 So the desire for wisdom brings to the Kingdom.
Wisdom is glorious, and never fadeth away: yea, she is easily seen of them that love her, and found of those who seek her. [12]

Here the wise man declares the nature of wisdom: on one side it is glorious, and its glories are not temporary but permanent and eternal, not fading. And on the other side it seeks after man, and announces its presence, and reveals itself to whoever loves it. It is easy to obtain and exceedingly simple, and ever present.
Truly it does not force itself, nor occupy a man’s heart by compulsion against his will; if he seeks it and asks for it, he finds it before him, longing to dwell in him.
Here he speaks of wisdom as being the Second Hypostasis, the divine Word, the Glorious, whose glory is everlasting and present in every place, whose delight is to abide in us while we abide in Him.

entries.section: 2. Wisdom comes to meet man

paragraphs.text: She goes before, and makes herself known to those who desire her. [13]
Along with the wonderful splendor of wisdom and its surpassing freshness, that is, its unceasing fruitfulness, those who love it and seek it recognize it, knowing it by practical experience and life.

He did not say that we are able to know wisdom, but that it makes itself known to whoever desires it. For man by his natural human abilities is unable to know divine wisdom. No one can say that Christ is Lord but by the Holy Spirit. No one experiences the sweetness of God’s wisdom and His powers and possibilities except him in whose heart love is poured out by the Holy Spirit (Rom 5:5).
Whoever possesses the Lord Christ knows Him and lives by Him and enjoys His divine wisdom, and truly becomes His ambassador.

entries.section: 2. Wisdom comes to meet man

paragraphs.text: And whoever seeks her early shall not labor much, for he shall find her sitting at his doors. [14]

The wise man calls us to long for wisdom and seek it, that it may be manifested in our hearts as on Mount Tabor. The secret of our weariness and our inability to discover the person of the Lord Christ and enjoy Him is that we do not rise early to Him. “I love them that love me; and those that seek me early shall find me” (Prov 8:17). Let Him be first in our hearts, our thoughts and our senses; no one and nothing shall occupy His place in us.

Wisdom, or the Lord Christ, on His part sits at our inner doors asking permission to enter. “Behold, I stand at the door, and knock: if any man hear my voice, and open the door, I will come in to him, and will sup with him, and he with me” (Rev 3:20).

* God gave us the Holy Spirit as an ally and mighty guardian, a great teacher of the Church, and a strong champion to help us. So do not fear the devils nor Satan, for He who fights for us is stronger than they.
Let us open our doors to Him, for He seeks those who deserve Him and searches out those to whom He is able to give His gifts.

St. Cyril of Jerusalem: Wisdom calls us to rise early in seeking Him, for none of the people in the wilderness could enjoy the manna that came down from heaven unless he rose early and gathered it before the rising of the sun.

He went before and took the initiative in love, He came to us Himself. In love He asks of the human soul, saying: “Open to me, my sister, my love, my dove, my undefiled: for my head is filled with dew, and my locks with the drops of the night” (Song 5:2). So if she despises Him, and prefers sleep to Him, and in sluggishness refuses to leave her bed to open the door to Him, she loses the opportunity of meeting Him, and we say: “I opened to my beloved; but my beloved had withdrawn himself, and was gone: my soul went out when he turned away: I sought him, but I could not find him; I called him, but he gave me no answer” (Song 5:6).

entries.section: 2. Wisdom comes to meet man

paragraphs.text: For meditation upon her is the perfection of wisdom, and whoever watches for her sake shall quickly be free from cares. [15]

Let us open our inner doors to our Savior by our solitude in quietness, contemplating our need of Him, and asking Him to enter and reveal Himself in us. We watch and refuse to sleep, saying with our father Jacob: “I will not let thee go, except thou bless me” (Gen 32:26).

For the way to wisdom is in our hands, indeed within us, and enjoying it is exceedingly easy, if we rise early to it, and forget everything for its sake. And we listen to its voice before every other voice.

The wise man asks of us a life of spiritual watchfulness, that is, concern for cleaving to the Lord, so that care cannot cleave to us, but we are freed from it and become in fellowship with the heavenly ones.

entries.section: 2. Wisdom comes to meet man

paragraphs.text: For she it is who goes about seeking those who are worthy of her, and in the ways appears to them with kindness, and in every thought of theirs comes to meet them. [16]

The wise man affirms the truth of the surpassing divine love, for though the divine Wisdom does not force our souls against our will, yet He stands at the door asking to enter into us. We on our part rise early to Him, declaring our desire to receive Him, and He on His part goes about as one searching for us, and appears to us in the midst of all our circumstances like one in the midst of the roads asking us to receive Him, and even declares Himself in our thoughts that we may long for it and desire His dwelling in us.

entries.section: 2. Wisdom comes to meet man

paragraphs.text: For the very true beginning of her is the sincere desire for discipline, and the care of discipline is love. [17]
The wise man offers us the ladder by which we ascend to enjoy wisdom; the five rungs of the ladder are:

a. Accepting discipline: The believer who longs for wisdom hates sin, and so accepts with joy what befalls him of discipline by divine permission, until sin becomes bitter in his mouth and he finds no pleasure in it.

b. By accepting the Lord’s discipline of him in sincerity and simplicity of heart, his heart opens more to the love of God. So the pleasures of the world do not occupy him, nor is he troubled by the toils of temporal life, but all his energies are absorbed in divine love.
c. As he loves God he keeps His commandments, and as the Lord Christ says: “He that hath my commandments, and keepeth them, he it is that loveth me” (Jn 14:13).
d. Whoever keeps the divine commandment, the commandment keeps him, so he bears the righteousness of Christ and appears before the Father justified freely, in purity and cleanness.
e. As the believer enjoys purity he cleaves to the Lord and sees Him. “Blessed are the pure in heart: for they shall see God” (Mt 5:8).

entries.section: 2. Wisdom comes to meet man

paragraphs.text: And love is the keeping of her laws, and the observing of the laws is the assurance of incorruption. [18]

entries.section: 2. Wisdom comes to meet man

paragraphs.text: And incorruption makes us draw near to God. [19]
Wisdom grants people immortality and fellowship in the Kingdom of God.
Nothing occupies the heart of the wise man like drawing near to God and being with Him eternally, so he often speaks of immortality and incorruption, or non-death, in eternal life.

* Man is mortal by nature, because he was created from nothing, yet because he was created in the image of the One who is, it was possible for him to resist the power of natural corruption and remain in incorruption, had he kept God in his knowledge, as Wisdom says: “The keeping of the laws brings about incorruption” (Wis 6:18). And by being in a state of incorruption it was possible for him to live from then on as God (immortal), as the Holy Bible indicates when it says: “I have said, Ye are gods; and all of you are children of the most High. But ye shall die like men, and fall like one of the princes” (Ps 82:6-7).

entries.section: 2. Wisdom comes to meet man

paragraphs.text: St. Athanasius the Apostolic: Therefore the desire for wisdom leads to the Kingdom. [20]

* These emotions (longings) are evil if the love is evil, and good if the love is good. Let us prove this from the Holy Bible. The Apostle desires to depart and be with Christ (Phil 1:23). And it is said: “My soul breaketh for the longing that it hath unto thy judgments” (Ps 119:20). And also: “The desire (longing) for wisdom leads to the Kingdom” (Wis 6:20).

entries.section: 2. Wisdom comes to meet man

paragraphs.text: St. Augustine: If your delight be then in thrones and sceptres, O ye kings of the people, honor wisdom, that ye may reign for evermore. [21]
The wise man directs the eyes of kings to the eternal Kingdom, and its way is the enjoyment of wisdom.

Truly He set us up for God here to be kings and masters, but as we experience what we have of spiritual authority and possibilities in Christ Jesus, our heart is lifted up to heaven that we may enjoy with the King of kings and Lord of lords the heavenly royal glories.
Here we reign where we have authority over thought, heart, tongue and all the senses, and this is a pledge of the true heavenly Kingdom.
The wise man directs the eyes of kings to the eternal Kingdom: “that you may reign forever”?

Since some groups attacked the Old Testament and claimed that it did not point to the eternal Kingdom of Heaven, St. Augustine pointed to the passage before us along with other passages he cited from the Old Testament to affirm his call to the eternal Kingdom.

* It was truly said: “Love wisdom, that you may reign forever” (cf. Wis 6:21). If eternal life had not been clearly known in the Old Testament, the Lord would not have said to the unbelieving Jews: “Search the scriptures; for in them ye think ye have eternal life: and they are they which testify of me” (Jn 5:39). And to the same end came the words of the Psalmist: “I shall not die, but live, and declare the works of the LORD” (Ps 118:17). Again he says: “Lighten mine eyes, lest I sleep the sleep of death” (Ps 12:3). Again we read: “The souls of the righteous are in the hand of the Lord, and no torment shall touch them” (Wis 3:1). And immediately follows: “They are in peace, and though they suffered torment from men, their hope is full of immortality, and after a few chastisements they shall have great reward.” Again he says in another place: “But the righteous live for evermore; their reward also is with the Lord, and the care of them is with the most High: therefore shall they receive a glorious kingdom, and a beautiful crown from the Lord’s hand” (Wis 5:15-16).
These passages and many like them about eternal life, with greater or less plainness, are found in these writings. Even the resurrection of the body the prophets spoke of.
St. Augustine

entries.section: 3. Solomon describes wisdom

paragraphs.text: 22 If your delight be then in the throne and sceptre, O ye kings of the people, honor wisdom, that ye may reign for evermore, 23 and love the light of wisdom, ye that be rulers of the people. 24 And I will tell you what wisdom is, and how she came up, and I will not hide the mysteries from you, but I will seek her out from the beginning of her nativity, and make the knowledge of her plain, and not pass over any part of the truth, 25 neither will I go with consuming envy, for such a man shall have no portion in wisdom. 26 The multitude of the wise is the salvation of the world, and the wise king the upholding of the people, 27 therefore be instructed by my words, and profit by them.
And I will tell you what wisdom is, and how she came up, and I will not hide the mysteries from you.
But I will seek her out from the beginning of her nativity, and make the knowledge of her plain, and not turn aside from the truth. [22]

The writer identifies himself as Solomon who enjoyed the gift of wisdom, and so he cannot hide its mysteries, lest he be counted ungrateful for God’s gift, or one who does not love his brethren. He desires that every person get to know it, love it, ask for it from God its source, and possess it with him!
The true wise man walks in righteousness, in whose heart there is no place for selfishness, so he desires that all share with him in what he has received.

Wisdom is a spring of living waters; the more others drink from it, the more the spring keeps the purity of its water as it overflows without ceasing, so its water does not become stagnant, exposed to pollution with algae and microbes.

The writer wishes to reveal the Wisdom that comes from God, because confusion has occurred in the thoughts of many people, so they consider pleasure to be the happy life, and consequently wisdom is made to consist in the pleasures of the body and the enjoyment of temporal gifts and amusement, while the divine and heavenly things are in their minds imagination and illusion, which make man lose his reason and wisdom.

* The ordinary definition of wisdom is the seeking of what is good and the avoiding of evil. Therefore the Apostle is right in describing the wisdom of the flesh (as enmity against God) as a longing for goods that do not remain with man, where there is fear of losing these things one day when he leaves them behind. Such wisdom cannot be subject to the law of God. It must be crushed so that the wisdom of the Spirit may take its place, which does not place its hope in earthly goods and does not fear worldly evils. For the one nature of the soul has the wisdom of the flesh when it seeks the lower things, as it has the wisdom of the Spirit when it seeks the higher things, like the one nature of water, which freezes in the cold and melts in the heat.
St. Augustine: * As long as the flesh lives... no believer can delight in the will of God and carry it out actively in his life.

St. Gregory of Nyssa: * Fleshly wisdom is death, for sin is grave, and through sin death came. It is called wisdom though it is folly. For to worldly people sin, whether in thought or in deed, is counted wisdom, recognized as such although it is against the law of God, especially since those who sin are full of activity and intelligence.

entries.section: 1. Wisdom is a helper for all

paragraphs.text: 1 She reaches from one end to the other with strength, and orders all things with gentleness.
She extends with power from the farthest end of the world to its farthest end, and orders all things well. [1]

The divine wisdom is the source of the order of the world, for He is a God of order and not of confusion (1 Cor 14:33), yet this order is offered for the edification of man. St. Augustine often used this phrase to affirm the care of God's wisdom wherever we may be, and His constant ordering of things for our sake.

* The Word of God, who is also the Son of God, co-eternal with the Father, the power of God and the wisdom of God (1 Cor 1:24). He extends by His might in a harmony that orders all things, from the greatest in intelligence to the least of material creation, creation visible and hidden, without being limited or divided or enlarged, but is present in His entirety without having any dimensions.

* What then, brethren? "All things were made by him." By this we have understood that all creation was made through the Son. The Father made it by His Word; God made it by His power and wisdom. Can we say that when He created things "all things were made by him," but that now the Father does not do all things through Him? God forbid! Let such thoughts be driven far from the hearts of believers. Let them be driven far from the thoughts of the devout and the understanding of the religious! It cannot be that the Father created through Him but did not order creation through Him. God forbid that He should not order what He brought into being, those things that were created through Him and received their existence through Him! See from the testimony of Holy Scripture itself that not only were all things created through Him, if we quote from the Gospel "All things were made by him; and without him was not any thing made that was made," but that all the things that were made are also ordered and arranged through Him. You know that Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God; know also what has been said of wisdom: "She extends from one end to the other with strength, and orders (with might) all things well" (Wis 8:1). So let us not doubt that all things are ordered through Him by whom all things were made. Thus the Father does nothing without the Son, nor the Son without the Father.

St. Augustine. Some ask: If the Son was sent into the world, was He not in the world before this mission was accomplished? He was in the world by the power of His divinity, but His mission concerns His incarnation, that He might accomplish salvation by the Cross and the Resurrection.

* He came into the world, and He was in the world. So He was sent to where He already was. Note also what was written through the prophet: "Do not I fill heaven and earth? saith the LORD" (Jer 23:24)... He who says, "I fill heaven and earth," was in every place... If it is said that this concerns the Father, how could the Father exist without His Word and without His wisdom, which "reaches with power from one end of the world to the other, and orders all things sweetly" (Wis 8:1)?

St. Augustine. He is the author of order and of providence, through which we touch not only the greatness of His power but also the sweetness of His love, which works for our sake in this ordering of the universe. He desires to keep the order working for our sake, yet He may break one of the natural laws if that is for our edification. In His love He does this, not to display His miracles, signs and wonders, but to proclaim His love and tenderness and the sweetness of His ordering of all things for our sake.
St. Augustine often used this phrase to affirm the presence of God in every place, and His continual care and providence in every place.

The appearing of God to Moses on Mount Sinai, where there was fire and smoke (Ex 19:18-19), does not mean that God, whether the Holy Trinity or one of the hypostases, was limited in His presence to one particular place and not another. It was so that Moses might be able to see God that He appeared thus in a particular place and in a manner in which He could be seen. But He is present in the whole world.

We do not wonder when we read: "And mount Sinai was altogether on a smoke, because the LORD descended upon it in fire" (Ex 19:18). And also: "And they saw the God of Israel: and there was under his feet as it were a paved work of a sapphire stone" (Ex 24:10).

Also in God's saying to Moses, "Thou shalt see my back parts: but my face shall not be seen" (Ex 33:23), and when the Apostle Paul says that we shall see Him face to face (1 Cor 13:12), and the saying of the Apostle John: "but we know that, when he shall appear, we shall be like him; for we shall see him as he is" (1 Jn 3:2). These expressions and the like do not mean that God has members, or can be divided, or exists in one place and not in another, but it is a condescension on His part so that we may enjoy Him and be able to see Him and speak with Him.

Again, when St. Augustine spoke of the snares that Satan sets for men, he said that the wisdom of God extends over all the world and orders all things sweetly, so that it turns the evils and plots of the devil into the benefit and glory of man.

entries.section: 2. Wisdom is an ideal bride

paragraphs.text: 2 I loved her and sought her out from my youth, and desired to take her for my bride, and I became a lover of her beauty. 3 For in her noble birth there is glory, because she lives with God, and the Lord of all has loved her, and she is the one whom I loved and sought from my youth, and strove to take her for my bride, and became a lover of her beauty. [2]
Wisdom is not acquired by human effort alone, but is given as a gift of God.

* From the will springs wisdom, with which the wise man enters into marriage, saying: "I sought to take her for my bride" (Wis 8:2). This will, which was formerly weak and lukewarm with the fever of diverse desires, rose up afterward, through the ministry of the Apostles, strong for the service of Christ.

St. Ambrose. * It is Solomon who says that he longs to make wisdom his bride (Wis 8:2). And in another place he says again of wisdom: "Love her, and she will embrace you; embrace her, and she will keep you" (cf. Prov 4:6, 8). Let us also take her to ourselves as a wife! Let us hold her in our arms, and not let her leave our embrace, nor let her flee from our arms. If this bride is always in our bosom, we shall beget children from her (that is, the fruit of the Spirit and not of the flesh).
St. Jerome. Origen sees that Sarah points to wisdom, so that Abraham, the righteous man of God, clung to her as his princess bride, to whom he listens in all that she says.

* I believe that "Sarah," which means "a ruling princess," represents arete, which is the virtue of the soul. This virtue, then, accompanies the wise and faithful man and clings to him, exactly as the wise man said of wisdom: "I desired to take her to me for a wife" (Wis 8:2). For this reason the Lord said to Abraham: "In all that Sarah hath said unto thee, hearken unto her voice" (Gen 21:12). This saying, however, does not suit bodily marriage, for it is known that the word was declared from heaven to the woman: [Your refuge shall be to him, and he shall rule over you] (cf. Gen 3:16). If the husband is said to be the lord of his wife, how is it said to Abraham, "In all that Sarah hath said unto thee, hearken unto her voice"? But if he is married to virtue, then in all that she counsels him, let him listen to her.

* In fact, God distinguishes the progress of the saints by likening it to marriage. You too, if you wish, can become a husband of this kind. For example, if you practice hospitality, you will seem to have taken this virtue as a wife. If you add to that compassion for the poor, you have a second wife. But if you also acquire patience and gentleness and the other virtues, you will seem to have as many wives as the virtues you have acquired.

entries.section: 2. Wisdom is an ideal bride

paragraphs.text: Origen. She glorifies her noble origin by her sharing in the life of God, and the Lord of all has loved her. [3]
What is the noble origin of wisdom, if not that she is the Second Divine Hypostasis, begotten of the Father from eternity, Light from Light, true God from true God, one with Him in the same essence?

This is the wisdom of God who became incarnate in order to reflect upon us dignity and honor from His noble origin, for being the only-begotten Son He gave us sonship to the Father in the waters of Baptism by His Holy Spirit, so that we have come to glory in this sonship.
As for wisdom's sharing in the life of the Father, the Lord Christ Himself says to the Father: "And all mine are thine, and thine are mine" (Jn 17:9).

By His incarnation He offered us the life of communion with God, by our union with the Father in the Holy Spirit through the merit of the shed blood of the Lord Christ. We have gained the right to enjoy heavenly and divine things as divine gifts that we receive through our reconciliation with the Father by the Cross.

As for the love of the Lord of all for wisdom, the Lord Christ says: "for thou lovedst me before the foundation of the world" (Jn 17:24); and He came to carry us to His Father so that we might enjoy His love. "That the love wherewith thou hast loved me may be in them, and I in them" (Jn 17:26).
It is as though the wise man asks us to acquire the wisdom of God, so that we may acquire the following:
A. The reflection of His noble origin upon us, so that He raises us from the dunghill to sit with the nobles of the nobles of His people.
B. Enjoyment of fellowship with God, or fellowship in the divine nature, so that we walk in the truth as children of God.
C. We carry wisdom, so that we truly become the object of God's surpassing love, and the possibility of loving God, the Lord of all, becomes ours.

entries.section: 3. Wisdom is the giver of riches

paragraphs.text: 4 For she is the initiate in the secrets of the knowledge of God, and the chooser of His works. 5 If riches are a precious possession in life, what is richer than wisdom, the maker of all things?
For she is acquainted with the knowledge of God, and the lover of His works. [4]
D. Enjoyment of the knowledge of God, which surpasses the human mind, for He reveals to us the divine mysteries.

Since wisdom is a divine hypostasis, "the wisdom of God," she cannot be separated from the Father, for He was never without wisdom. This wisdom, if one may say so, is the storehouses of the divine knowledge and His work and surpassing plan; she reveals the works of God and the surpassing mysteries behind them.

entries.section: 3. Wisdom is the giver of riches

paragraphs.text: If riches are a desirable possession, what is richer than wisdom, which works all things? [5]
E. Enjoyment of true riches, not transient temporal possessions, but the love of God and His care and providence that never cease.

The wisdom of God is not a static perception or theoretical knowledge, but is ever in motion, the inward movement of love, which also works all things, for she is creator, almighty and governor of all. She is not separated from the divine providence over all creation, heavenly and earthly.

entries.section: 4. Wisdom is at work in her companion

paragraphs.text: 6 And if prudence is that which works, who is more skilled than she in the design of the universe? 7 And if anyone loves righteousness, her labors are the virtues, for she teaches temperance and prudence and justice and fortitude, than which nothing in life is more profitable for men. 8 And if anyone longs for various kinds of knowledge, she knows the things of old and represents the future, and understands the arts of speech and the solving of riddles, and knows signs and wonders before they come to pass, and the events of seasons and times.
And if prudence is that which works, who is more skilled than she in the design of beings? [6]
F. Enjoyment of understanding and skill. God created man and gave him a mind able to invent, to discover and to progress continually. He is unique among all earthly creatures, always advancing.
Our enjoyment of the divine wisdom sanctifies the mind and gives strength and ability to work earnestly, so that man becomes truly skilled in the talents that God has given him.
Wisdom is the Creator, the Artist, the Architect of the universe. So when we are united with wisdom we carry the spirit of invention in humility.
"The LORD by wisdom hath founded the earth; by understanding hath he established the heavens. By his knowledge the depths are broken up, and the clouds drop down the dew" (Prov 3:19-20).

entries.section: 4. Wisdom is at work in her companion

paragraphs.text: And if a man loves righteousness, her labors are the virtues, for she teaches self-control and prudence and righteousness, and courage, than which nothing in life is more profitable for men. [7]

G. Enjoyment of the virtues. At the beginning of the book the wise man linked wisdom with practical righteousness. Now, as the wise man declares the desire of many to be righteous, there is no way to enjoy the righteous, virtuous life except by acquiring divine wisdom.
Divine wisdom produces in the children of God four important and principal practical virtues: 1. Contentment. 2. Prudence, or practical understanding. 3. Righteousness.

The Lord Christ, the incarnate wisdom, is called the "Sun of righteousness" (Mal 4:2). Whoever He rises upon, He enlightens and gives him surpassing righteousness, while those who do not enjoy His light are deprived of righteousness and live in the darkness of sin.

* Those upon whom the "Sun of righteousness" (Mal 4:2), that is, Christ, has not risen, and whose soul's eyes have not been opened and enlightened by the true light, are still under the same darkness of sin and under the same influence of the passions, and they are under the very same punishment, since they have not yet eyes with which to look upon the Father.
St. Macarius the Great. 4. Courage or patience:

God did not promise His believers who receive heavenly wisdom the broad, easy way and the pampered life, but promised them the narrow way, that they may share with Him His cross and His sufferings, and even His death. The spiritually wise man faces many wars from without as well as from within, but with the multitude of battles he enjoys mighty divine resources by which he overcomes and is crowned.

* The man who has truly renounced the world, and cast off the weight of this earth, and thrown off the vain fleshly lusts and the desires for human glory and honors, and has withdrawn from them all with all his heart... and has set firmly in his heart to serve the Lord and worship Him and cleave to Him with his whole being, body and soul, such a man, I say, discovers the presence of the opposition, that is, the hidden passions, and the unseen bonds and the hidden war, that is, the inner battle and struggle, and thus as he entreats the Lord he receives the heavenly armor, the armor of the Holy Spirit, which the blessed Apostle set forth by saying: "the breastplate of righteousness, the helmet of salvation, the shield of faith and the sword of the Spirit" (Eph 6:14). And being armed with these arms he is able to stand against the deceits of the devil even though he is surrounded by evils... he becomes able to war against the principalities of this world. And by his victory over the hostile powers with the help of the Holy Spirit, together with his striving and zeal in every virtue, he becomes prepared for eternal life.

St. Macarius the Great. St. Macarius the Great sees that God may delay the answer to prayer and the support of man quickly in his warfare, so that his longing for eternal goods may increase, and that he may train in patience and in striving courageously.

* He who does not receive grace quickly because of God's long-suffering burns the more with longing, and grows every day in desire and diligence, and increases in running and striving, and increases in every virtue, and shows hunger and thirst for what is good... and does not turn to contempt and despair and impatience. On the other hand, he does not give himself up to sloth under the guise of pretended patience, saying: "One day or another I shall obtain the grace of God"... but he ought to be more careful and diligent, and not weary or fail, but seek the gift of God, trusting that God is true and cannot lie, for it is He who promised to give His grace to those who seek in faith with all patience to the end.

St. Macarius the Great. Perhaps among the most wonderful stories of courage joined with wisdom is the stand of St. John Chrysostom in the year 387 A.D., when the Emperor Theodosius the Great imposed a new additional tax to meet the expense of the celebration of the tenth anniversary of the Emperor Theodosius' reign and the fifth anniversary of his young son Arcadius' sharing power with him.

The people of Antioch rose in revolt, for they knew the greed of the tax collectors and the abuse of such a decree, and many fled to the wilderness from the face of the tax collectors. The people took refuge with the governor, who could not intercede for them with the Emperor for fear for his position. They took refuge with the archbishop Flavian (Flavianus), but because of his old age he evaded the situation.

Amid popular crowds of every kind, cries soon spread, bringing forth agitation and then revolt. In the twinkling of an eye, without any thought and without any restraint, some went off to smash the statues of the Emperor and the Empress and their son, and threw them into the mud and the filth.

All this took place in moments full of the heat of revolt, followed by a calm in which they came to themselves from their drunkenness and felt the hideousness of their crime, and became afraid, expecting their fate and the fate of their city to be severe punishment. The whole city was in confusion, great and small, and no one knew what should be done.

The order was issued to burn the whole city, but St. John the priest urged the high priest to travel a distance of more than a thousand kilometers to meet the Emperor and obtain pardon from him, as Moses the prophet did when he interceded before God (Ex 32:32). He asked him not to return without this pardon. Most likely he prepared for him what he should say before the Emperor in a spirit of humility, but with strength and courage. The holy priest stood and said to the people: "Your bishop has set out like a courageous young man who has two wings... I am sure that the mere appearance of the bishop before the pious Emperor will calm the fury of his anger against us, for divine grace shines forth not only from the words of the saint, but in his face also."

In a spirit of courage the bishop said to the Emperor: "Your crown, O lord of Rome and the world, is magnificent. It is a proof of your worthiness, but it signifies the generosity of the one who conferred it upon you. But the crown of your humanity owes its merit to your wisdom alone. Men admire the shining precious stones upon your brow, how much more will they admire the victory you win over your heart!" He assured him that if he pardoned the Antiochenes he would gain great glory that the passing of generations would not erase, and he said to him: "Great multitudes will join the Christian religion, saying: Behold the Christian religion, it has quenched the wrath of a man who has no equal in the world."

The patriarch, or bishop of Antioch, reached Constantinople, and hastened to the royal court in spite of his great weariness, and met the Emperor and said to him: "I am not a messenger of the people of Antioch, but also an ambassador of God. I have come to you in His name to announce to you: If you forgive men their trespasses and their faults, your heavenly Father will forgive you your trespasses and your faults... Remember that dreadful day when we shall all be bound to give account of our works... All the ambassadors appear before you with the splendor of gold and the multitude of gifts and the abundance of money, but I offer you nothing but the holy law of Jesus Christ, and the example He gave us on the Cross that we might deserve the forgiveness of our sins..."

The Emperor's heart was filled with the fear of the Lord when he heard this speech, and he said: "If our Lord and Master Jesus Christ became a servant for our sake, and gave Himself up to the Cross, and asked His Father to forgive those who crucified Him, how then shall I dare to hesitate in forgiving my enemies?"
St. Jerome sees that these four virtues which God offers us are the horses that draw the chariot that lifts us up to heaven.

* Let these four be the pillars of your horizon, and let them be the four horses that work together to carry you, the chariot of Christ, which runs at its utmost speed to bring you to the goal. There is no necklace more precious than this, nor any jewel more brilliant than this galaxy of stars. They are your adornment, encircling you and protecting you on every side. They are your line of defense and your glory, for every jewel of them is turned into a shield!

St. Jerome. In a letter that St. Jerome sent to the senator Pammachius, he mentioned that the members of the household of the one to whom he wrote enjoy these four traits, but while each member enjoys all the traits, each one has a particular trait in which he excels, for he wrote to him: [Each of you possesses the four (virtues), but each has one that is distinctive. You are distinguished by prudence, your mother by righteousness, your virgin sister by endurance (patience), and your wife by contentment. I speak of you as wise, for who can be wiser than he who despises the foolishness of the world and follows Christ, the power of God and the wisdom of God (1 Cor 1:24)?]

entries.section: 4. Wisdom is at work in her companion

paragraphs.text: And if anyone desires wide experience, she knows the past and foretells the future, and is skilled in the framing of proverbs and the solving of riddles, and knows signs and wonders before they happen, and the succession of seasons and times. [8]

Enjoyment of the Lord Christ lifts man above nature, and carries him to the past, not as a time that has passed and ended but into a life and experience where he finds in his past God's surpassing favors toward him, and his soul rejoices. And he enjoys the present like one at a wedding, in union with the heavenly Bridegroom, and as for the future, it is not unknown to him, for he sees his Christ preparing for him surpassing eternal glories. In other words, he sees in the past a life rejoicing in the Lord and in the future opened heavens.

In other words, the Lord Christ adds to man's lifetime a surpassing life, so that the day becomes for him like a thousand years, and he counts every moment of his life as having its own account, since He adds to his mortal temporal life the eternal life of the Lord Christ.

Besides these surpassing gifts, the wisdom of God gives him a sanctified mind, so that there are no obscure riddles in his life, but his life becomes a straight and clear way by which he passes into the Father's bosom.

In the love of the divine wisdom for us, she hides nothing from us so long as it is for our benefit and edification, so that we perceive surpassing mysteries that spring from the mystery of God's love for us.

In brief, the wisdom of God offers us mighty resources to cross the valley of tears while we are in His bosom, finding His cross sweet and experiencing the power of His resurrection, and enjoying heavenly things, as though our heart had ascended with Him and refused to part from Him.

entries.section: 5. A bride who gives glory on earth and in heaven

paragraphs.text: 9 Therefore I determined to take her to me to live with me, knowing that she would be to me a counselor of good things, and a comfort in cares and grief. 10 Because of her I shall have glory among the multitudes, and honor in the presence of the elders, though I am young. 11 And I shall be counted keen in judgment, and shall be admired in the presence of the mighty. 12 When I am silent they will wait for me, and when I speak they will give heed, and when I continue in speaking they will lay their hands upon their mouths. 13 Because of her I shall obtain immortality, and leave behind me an everlasting memory to those who come after me. 14 I shall govern peoples, and nations will be subject to me. 15 Dread monarchs will hear and fear me; among the multitude I shall be seen to be good, and in war courageous. 16 When I enter my house, I shall find rest with her, for there is no bitterness in her company, nor pain in living with her, but gladness and joy.
Therefore I determined to take her to be the companion of my life, knowing that she would be to me a counselor of good, and a strengthener in cares and grief. [9]

Solomon the wise says: "Wisdom is good with an inheritance: and by it there is profit to them that see the sun" (Eccl 7:11). And also: "When wisdom entereth into thine heart, and knowledge is pleasant unto thy soul; discretion shall preserve thee, understanding shall keep thee" (Prov 2:10-11).

He had already spoken of his seeking to take wisdom as a bride, loving her spiritual beauty and rejoicing in union with her (Wis 8:2). Now he speaks of her as the companion of his life, who occupies the seat of command within him, counseling him to good, and supporting and strengthening him in the midst of afflictions and griefs.

The wise man says: "woe to him that is alone when he falleth; for he hath not another to help him up" (Eccl 4:10). What then if this second is the Lord Christ, the wisdom of God, dwelling within him, able to raise up even from death, and to grant immortality even if the body is corrupted!

entries.section: 5. A bride who gives glory on earth and in heaven

paragraphs.text: So because of her I shall have glory among the multitudes, and honor in the presence of the elders in spite of my youth. [10]

Ahasuerus asked Vashti the beautiful queen to appear at a licentious banquet, so that he might boast of her beauty. But the believer boasts of the true beauty, the wisdom of God, fairer than the children of men. The secret of the believer's glory, honor and power is the wisdom of God, which directs his whole inner life.

It is said of a Greek king that he said one day: This child rules the world. And when those present were astonished, they asked him: How is this? The king answered: "Greece rules the world, and Athens rules Greece, and I rule Athens, and my wife rules me, and this child rules my wife!" Thus the king points to the hidden power of the family, how such a child has an influence upon the world.
If such a child rules the world, how great is the work of the Lord Christ of whom we speak, who is able to direct our whole life!

By handing over the steering wheel to wisdom, he enters into a glorious life among the multitudes, so that circumstances, whatever they may be, cannot spoil his inner glory or take away his honor. He bears the marks of the wise elders in spite of his young age.

entries.section: 5. A bride who gives glory on earth and in heaven

paragraphs.text: And they will find me keen in the administration of judgment, and will admire me in the presence of the great. [11]
Solomon the wise was known for his ability to decide cases with rare wisdom.
It is said of the virtuous woman that her husband is known in the gates when he sitteth among the elders of the land (Prov 31:23), judging cases.

Thus he who is united with the Lord Christ, the giver of virtue, enjoys the ability to sit among the elders to pass judgments through the grace of his heavenly Bridegroom. And the son of Sirach says: "Many shall commend his understanding; and so long as the world endureth, it shall not be blotted out; his memorial shall not depart away, and his name shall live from generation to generation. Nations shall declare his wisdom, and the congregation shall show forth his praise. If he die, he shall leave a greater name than a thousand: and if he live, he shall increase it" (Sir 39:9-11).

entries.section: 5. A bride who gives glory on earth and in heaven

paragraphs.text: And when I am silent they will wait for me, and when I speak they will give heed, and if I continue in speaking, they will lay their hands upon their mouths. [12]

When the believer enjoys union with the wisdom of God, his silence, like his words, turns to edification. If the wise man is silent, there is in his silence an eloquent speech that the hearts and minds of those present understand. They do not tire of his silence, but find in his silence blessings that come upon them, and at the same time they await his words as though they were precious jewels worthy of every esteem and honor.

The wise man says: "The words of a man's mouth are as deep waters, and the wellspring of wisdom as a flowing brook" (Prov 18:4). If the wise man speaks they listen to him, because the speaker is the Lord working in him, and however much he pours forth words they ask for more. They lay their hands upon their mouths as a sign of their silence in reverence and respect for the speaker (Job 29:9). They do not speak, not out of fear of him, nor because he refuses dialogue, but so that they may use every moment for him to speak.

entries.section: 5. A bride who gives glory on earth and in heaven

paragraphs.text: And because of her I shall obtain immortality, and leave behind me to those who come after me an everlasting memory. [13]

The wise man had already declared that righteousness is immortal, so whoever acquires wisdom acquires righteousness, and whoever acquires righteousness lives with the Holy One forever. Even before the coming of the Day of Judgment the life of the wise remains a memorial through the generations from which many benefit.

* Who dares to refuse to acknowledge that He (the Lord Christ) is immortal, if He Himself makes others immortal? For it is written of the wisdom of God: "Through her I shall obtain immortality" (cf. Wis 8:13). But His immortality according to His nature is one thing, and our immortality is another. There is no comparison between what is perishable and the divine.

Divinity alone is the essence that death cannot touch. For this reason the Apostle, although he knows that the human soul and the angels are immortal, declares that God alone has immortality (1 Tim 6:17).

entries.section: 5. A bride who gives glory on earth and in heaven

paragraphs.text: St. Ambrose. I shall govern peoples, and nations will be subject to me. [14]

The wise man had already declared that God created man to rule the world in holiness and righteousness. By wisdom the believer governs peoples and nations are subject to him, not through civil or military authority, but through the authority of the Spirit, since many desire to follow his example, and his conduct and life become a constitution for them.

By wisdom all man's energies and abilities are subjected and work together in marvelous harmony, so that the believer lives like a king with authority over his depths of emotions, thoughts and feelings.

entries.section: 5. A bride who gives glory on earth and in heaven

paragraphs.text: Dread kings will hear of me and fear, and I shall appear good among the multitude, and brave in war. [15]
Wisdom pours upon us a kind of awe, so that kings and great men fear the righteous wise man, because he is a man of God.

The wise man is marked by meekness, so the multitudes love him, and along with meekness he is also marked by courage and patience, so he does not fear the opposition of others against him, but says: "If an army rises against me I will not fear evil."

entries.section: 5. A bride who gives glory on earth and in heaven

paragraphs.text: And when I enter my house I shall rest beside her, for there is no bitterness in her company, nor any pain in living with her, but gladness and joy. [16]

The dwelling of the Lord Christ in the family gives it gladness and joy. Each member deals with the other members in Christ Jesus, and all compete in giving and bestowing, not in taking and dominating. The family is transformed into a holy church filled with peace and exultation.

entries.section: 6. Wisdom is an immortal bride

paragraphs.text: 17 So when I thought upon these things in myself, and considered in my heart that in kinship with wisdom there is immortality, 18 and in her friendship a good pleasure, and in the labors of her hands unfailing riches, and in the exercise of intimacy with her prudence, and in sharing in her conversation renown, I went about seeking how to take her to myself. 19 Now I was a child of good disposition, and I was given a good soul, 20 or rather, being good, I came into a body undefiled. 21 But when I knew that I could not be chaste unless God gave me chastity, and it was a mark of prudence to know from whom this gift came, I turned to the Lord and besought Him with my whole heart, saying:
And after I had thought about these things within myself, and considered in my heart that in being near to wisdom there is immortality. [17]

Solomon thought within himself that the nobility of his birth as a son of King David is not what prepares him to obtain wisdom, but she is a divine gift, requiring that he draw near to God in prayer and ask Him to receive her. And by receiving wisdom nothing more occupies him except through his enjoyment of eternity (immortality).

By our drawing near to the Lord Christ and entering into fellowship with Him, our heart is lifted up to heaven, and we experience its earnest. We say with the Apostle Paul: "made us sit with him in the heavenly places" (Eph 2:6).
"The heart" among the Jews points to the throne of thought and understanding, as we have already pointed out, while the Greeks use the expression "mind Nous" to express thought and understanding.

entries.section: 6. Wisdom is an immortal bride

paragraphs.text: And in her friendship is pure pleasure, and in the labors of her hands unfailing riches, and in the experience of intimacy with her prudence, and in conversing with her a good reputation, I went about seeking how I might take her to myself. [18]

When the soul cleaves to the Lord Christ, man enters with Him into a delightful, exalted friendship. He will not suffer from the feeling of isolation, even if all forsake him. It is as though he says with his Savior: "ye shall leave me alone: and yet I am not alone, because the Father is with me."
Our cleaving to Him urges us to work and strive, and we count all labor as riches and glory, because we work with Him and by Him and for Him. So our sufferings bear a touch of inward sweetness.

Our cleaving to Him pours prudence upon us, so that along with walking in simplicity of heart like little children we carry the wisdom of elders, or as the Lord Christ says: "Be ye therefore wise as serpents, and harmless as doves," so simplicity is joined with wisdom and understanding.
Our cleaving to Him drives us to humility, because He humbled Himself for us, and in His humility He lifted us up and poured upon us surpassing honor.

In view of all these gifts, the enjoyment of heavenly things and the delightful friendship and the sweetness amid striving, and wisdom and understanding with simplicity, and the pouring out of inward glory and honor and a good reputation even among the heavenly ones, who would not go about seeking to cleave to Him? Therefore the human soul says of her heavenly Bridegroom, the wisdom of God: "I found him whom my soul loveth: I held him, and would not let him go, until I had brought him into my mother's house, and into the chamber of her that conceived me" (Song 3:4).

entries.section: 6. Wisdom is an immortal bride

paragraphs.text: I was a child of good disposition, and I was given a good soul, [19]

The writer returns to the first state of man at his creation, for God created man a good being, "So God created man in his own image, in the image of God created he him; male and female created he them" (Gen 1:27).

Here too the writer wishes to affirm that the body in itself is good and undefiled, since through the centuries many philosophies appeared that ascribe corruption to the body by its nature. For this reason the Fathers of the Church often affirm that the corruption of man springs from the corruption of his will and not from the nature of the body.

entries.section: 6. Wisdom is an immortal bride

paragraphs.text: But rather, being good, I came into a body undefiled. [20]

The writer does not mean here that the human soul has a pre-existence, and because it is good it received an undefiled body, but we understand it through the book as a whole: he wishes to affirm the leading role of the soul even over the body. The subject of original sin was not in the writer's mind at all.
Origen sees that the speaker here is Jesus Christ, who alone was in the womb of His mother with a body not from the seed of men, and bore in Himself no corruption of Adam.

entries.section: 6. Wisdom is an immortal bride

paragraphs.text: And when I knew that I could not be wise unless God gave her to me - and it was part of wisdom to know from whom this grace comes - I prayed to the Lord and besought Him, and said with my whole heart: [21]

The wise man spoke of his longing for wisdom and asked it of God, realizing that he could not enjoy her unless she were given to him by God. What he said here applies to every sincere and true virtue, because virtue is nothing but the enjoyment of fellowship with the Righteous Holy One.
This is what St. Augustine expressed in his Confessions when he spoke of chastity in the same spirit.
In a wonderful prayer St. Augustine speaks to God with the certainty that however difficult His commandments may seem, they are within reach of our hand, so long as God grants us to carry them out.

* All my hope is in Thy great and surpassing mercies. Give what Thou commandest, and command what Thou wilt. Thou dost impose chastity upon us. One says: "And when I knew that I could not obtain her except God gave her... this is wisdom, to know from whom this grace comes.

* You seek wisdom, my son, that you may be steadfast in this race, for you entered upon it from the beginning under the influence of wisdom. Let it be part of your wisdom to know from whom this grace (gift) comes. "Commit thy way unto the LORD; trust also in him; and he shall bring it to pass. And he shall bring forth thy righteousness as the light, and thy judgment as the noonday" (Ps 37:5-6).

* As for chastity, I thought it was within my power (though I did not find this power in me). I was foolish, for I did not know what is written: "No one can be chaste unless Thou give it," and that Thou wilt give it to me if I knock with my inward sighs at the door of Thine ears, and with right faith fix my attention upon Thee.

* Without doubt the value of the gift of chastity was known to the one who said: "I knew that no one can be chaste unless God give (this) gift." So he not only knew the greatness of the benefit of chastity, and how it must be longed for and desired, but that unless God gives it it cannot exist. Wisdom taught him this.

* He says: "And when I knew that no one can be chaste unless God give (chastity), and this is part of wisdom, to know from whom this gift (grace) comes" (Wis 8:21). These two gifts, wisdom and chastity, are great. Truly by wisdom we are formed according to the knowledge of God, and by chastity we are not conformed to this world.

* When He commands us, saying: "Go not after your lusts" (Sir 18:30), let us say to Him: "We know that no man can be chaste unless God give it to him" (cf. Wis 8:21); what do we say but: Give what Thou hast commanded.
* No one can be chaste unless God grants him this gift, nor is the love of God shed abroad in our hearts from ourselves, but by the Holy Ghost which is given unto us (Rom 5:5).
* Wisdom and chastity are the two gifts of God, that is, they are not from others.

* Certainly such commandments could not have been given if man did not have freedom of will, by which he obeys the divine commandments, for it is necessary for keeping the commandments of chastity. For this reason it is said in the Book of Wisdom: "I knew that no one can be chaste unless God give it to him - and it was part of wisdom to know from whom this grace comes" (cf. Wis 8:21).

* If even in the body, the least element of its nature, all the lofty things, such as beauty and vitality and health and so on, are the work of God, how much more are the lofty things that belong to the soul.

* It is a very great matter that we aim to speak of what He (God) gives, for in the first place we say and affirm that chastity is a gift from God (Wis 8:21). It is written in the Book of Wisdom that no one can be chaste unless God grants him this.
St. Augustine
May my soul be joined to You,

entries.section: 1. God sets man up as lord

paragraphs.text: 1 O God of the fathers, O Lord of mercy, who hast made all things by thy word, 2 and formed man by thy wisdom, that he should have dominion over the creatures which thou hast made, 3 and rule the world in holiness and righteousness, and execute judgment with an upright soul.
"O God of my fathers, and Lord of mercy, who hast made all things by thy word. [1]
At the beginning of his reign Solomon turns his face toward God to ask Him for the enjoyment of wisdom. Here he calls upon God with the following titles:

entries.section: A. God of the fathers

paragraphs.text: By the fathers he means the patriarchs Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and perhaps he also had in mind Noah and Moses the prophet and Joshua the son of Nun and some of the judges and King David and others. All of them were great leaders, each with his distinct personality, yet each one completes the others, for God is the supreme Leader of leaders.

He calls the leaders fathers, and God attributes Himself to the fathers: "God of the fathers." For leadership in the mind of Solomon the wise is nothing but fatherhood and tenderness and gentleness toward others, so that all become for him as those in the place of sons. He exercises leadership not from a position of authority with commands and prohibitions, but from the position of fatherhood!

If the Creator of heaven and earth presents Himself to His creation as the God of the fathers, how much more does it befit civil and religious leaders to open their hearts to others with a kind of fatherhood.

Leadership is not merely a position in the Church or the administration of certain works or merely rituals and duties carried out in any manner, but it is first and before everything fatherhood, which the servant receives as a gift from the Lord who called him.

And God, in offering fatherhood to His children the servants, offers them its essence and its pillar, love, without which we cannot taste the truth of fatherhood or feel its presence. He also trains His children and develops them in the school of love from childhood, that they may be like God, and not be harsh fathers who provoke their children and destroy them. For this reason we say that the only school from which the true servants of God graduate in the Old and New Testaments, which still is and will remain so until the faithful men of God graduate in it, is the school of Christian love.
* O teacher, intercessor of the divine mysteries, speak with love.
He who teaches and does not love is restrained by silence, for in vain he wearies himself composing unprofitable words.
The great master, if he wishes to win his hearers, let him love much and speak little with his disciples.
St. Jacob of Serugh. * I teach that the man who is placed over the community and rules over them is not supported and magnified by anything like showing deep love for those under him.

For a father is not a father merely because he begot sons but because he loves them. So if nature requires this love of necessity, how much more the sonship that is by grace? I mean, if a person must love his natural children in order to be called a natural father, how much more must he love his children according to grace, the spiritual ones who are baptized, lest they become punished in Gehenna.
St. John Chrysostom. * His coming (Christ's) has poured out upon mankind a great gift of fatherly grace.

St. Irenaeus. * How great is God's love for men! For He granted to those who had departed from Him and fallen into the abyss of vices the forgiveness of sins and an abundant share of grace, so that they call Him Father, saying: "Our Father which art in heaven." The heavens are those who bear the image of the heavenly world, and in whom God dwells and abides.
St. Cyril of Jerusalem

entries.section: B. Lord of mercy

paragraphs.text: Since Solomon is speaking with God, asking Him for the wisdom that gives him the spirit of fatherhood toward his people, and indeed toward every man, he calls God "Lord of mercy." For man cannot enjoy the spirit of tenderness and kindness and gentleness toward others unless the merciful God gives him this gift.

For mercy in its essence is not a passing emotion toward a suffering or needy person, but is a sharing in a characteristic particular to God, who is true "Love," the giver of mercy as an inward trait in the soul, so that man has mercy even on those who oppose him, as he has mercy on animals, and is gentle with everything.

* "Blessed are the merciful: for they shall obtain mercy"... He gave mercy to the merciful because they accept true and wonderful counsel, so that the One greater than they (God) deals with them in the same way in which they deal with those lesser than themselves: "Blessed are the merciful: for they shall obtain mercy."
St. Augustine. * Let us be merciful, as it is written, so that God may be merciful to us (Mt 5:7).

* Moses led the flock of Jethro his father-in-law, and was chosen from tending sheep to tend his people, and he led them as a good shepherd. Moses carried his rod on his shoulder, and went before his people whom he led, and shepherded them forty years, and he was watchful and toiled for his flock; he was a good shepherd. When his Lord wished to destroy them because of their sins, when they worshiped the calf, Moses prayed for them and asked his Lord, saying: "Yet now, if thou wilt forgive their sin; and if not, blot me, I pray thee, out of thy book which thou hast written" (Ex 32:32). This is the exceedingly watchful shepherd, who gives himself up for his flock. This is the excellent leader who lays down himself for his flock. This is the merciful father who embraces his sons and brings them up.
St. Aphrahat the Persian Sage

entries.section: C. Creator of all by His word:

paragraphs.text: Solomon directs his prayer to God, the Creator of all by His word or wisdom. It is not enough for the leader to be a merciful father, but he must imitate God the Creator who brought all things into being by His word, who is the wisdom of God. So the leader is to be prudent and wise.

For some do wrong even with regard to their own children, offering tenderness and burning emotion without prudence and without discernment and wisdom. For this reason Father Gregory (the Great) tells us that pastoral care or leadership is an art.

* It is true medicine when we treat a sickness that is in the body and at the same time heal the prevailing needs of the body. If the medicine of the body can be compounded and prescribed to serve different ends, is it not even more fitting for the medicine of the soul, which comes in the folds of one teaching and which is the art of the lofty arts, treating things that are not seen, to conquer the various moral evils?
* Treatment at the wrong time makes wounds more painful. And if the medicines are not suitable, they are certainly not fit for the purpose of healing.

* The shepherd of souls must discern with wisdom and care between virtues and vices, lest stinginess take hold of his heart while he exaggerates in appearing as a good manager, or lest he boast of his generosity as though it were a virtue when in truth he is a spendthrift and a destroyer. Or lest he overlook what he ought to criticize sharply, and so bring eternal punishment upon his flock, or punish faults without mercy, and so sin a greater sin, or when he spoils what he could have done with dignity and uprightness by his hasty and rash expectations. Likewise the postponing of a good deed may turn it into an evil deed.
Father Gregory (the Great)

entries.section: C. Creator of all by His word:

paragraphs.text: And formed man by thy wisdom, that he should have dominion over the creatures which thou hast made. [2]

entries.section: D. The divine Leader who raises up leaders, not slaves

paragraphs.text: The wise man stands in amazement before the wisdom of the Creator, which is manifested not only in creating man with this surpassing creativity, nor in His care for him in that He created the world for his sake, but, what is greater, in the wisdom He gave him to rule the earthly creation. It is marvelous that the Creator gives man this authority, and offers him wisdom, to raise him up as a leader to rule over the world. For God said to Adam, charging him and his wife and their descendants after them: "Have dominion over the fish of the sea, and over the fowl of the air, and over every living thing that moveth upon the earth, and every tree, in the which is the fruit of a tree yielding seed" (Gen 1:29).

entries.section: D. The divine Leader who raises up leaders, not slaves

paragraphs.text: And rule the world in holiness and righteousness, and execute judgment with an upright soul. [3]

E. The Holy and Righteous One raises up righteous saints who rule with justice and not with injustice. If God by His wisdom made man wise, knowing how to rule over creation, then, being the Holy and Righteous One without sin, He granted man to be holy and righteous so that he may rule the world in holiness and righteousness, and judge in all matters with an upright soul or an upright heart.

God set man up to be truly an icon of the Holy and Righteous One, and he himself becomes a temple of the Holy One without blemish, in which God dwells. Indeed he even desires to see all his brothers and sisters holy and righteous, so that each man and woman sees in everyone the dazzling image of God.
Thus nothing occupies the heart of the true believer like being holy and righteous in the Lord, and seeing all mankind become holy and righteous, blameless before God.

entries.section: 2. The need for divine wisdom

paragraphs.text: 4 Give me wisdom, that sitteth by thy throne; and reject me not from among thy children: 5 For I am thy servant and the son of thine handmaid, a feeble man and of a short time, and lacking in understanding of judgment and laws. 6 But if there be one perfect among the children of men, yet if thy wisdom be not with him, he shall be counted as nothing.
Give me wisdom, that sitteth with thee by thy throne, and cast me not off from among thy children. [4]
The wise man looked toward God, the giver of wisdom, and saw Him as:
· Father of the fathers, the giver of true fatherhood.
· Lord of mercy, the giver of tenderness and kindness.
· Creator by His word, and by His wisdom the giver of wisdom and discernment.
· The divine Leader, who raises up leaders and not slaves.
· The Holy One, who raises up saints as witnesses to Him, who rule with righteousness and holiness.
This is on God's side; what then is man's part, that he may enjoy the wisdom of God?

Here Solomon stands to see the wisdom of God, the Second Hypostasis seated on the throne, and who can reach Him? There is no way to cross over to Him, but by His humility He comes down to us, and in the spirit of humility we meet with Him to possess Him.

He is seated on the throne, but He is not far from us, for He takes the initiative with practical love, bows the heavens and comes down, to stand at the doors of our hearts asking to enter. He does not break into our hearts or our thoughts without our will, but waits for us to invite Him! For our part we realize that by His coming down He made us His sons, and opened for us the door of Baptism and paid the price by the Cross. We must ask Him in hope and boldness not to cast us off, for we are His sons.
He knocks at the doors of our hearts with His surpassing love and humility, and we knock at His doors with prayer in the spirit of humility, with hope and boldness!

If God created man to rule over creatures and to govern the world in holiness and righteousness, who can give him these resources but the wisdom that sits on the divine throne? She sets man up as a wise lord, able to act with power and wisdom, in holiness and righteousness. However great man's perfection and gifts and abilities and resources may be, without divine wisdom man is counted as nothing.

* Wisdom must be sought from God alone and not from philosophers or astrologers. God gives wisdom like a spring whose waters will not cease, and waters everyone who enters by it; but the wisdom of philosophers and other human agencies is not given generously, and soon dries up.

Hilary of Arles. * What blessing does that man not possess who seeks this wisdom and receives it from the Lord? This gives you understanding. What a grace this is; for if this wisdom were from ourselves it would not be from above, and we would not ask it from God who created us.

entries.section: 2. The need for divine wisdom

paragraphs.text: St. Augustine. For I am thy servant and the son of thine handmaid, a weak man and short-lived, with little understanding of judgment and laws. [5]

King Solomon confesses that he is a servant of the Lord and the son of His handmaid; what he receives from God is by His free grace and generous love, and not by personal merit. In the spirit of humility the king declares his inability to accomplish his mission with which God entrusted him, for his days are short and his understanding little, he has no knowledge nor learning nor experience, so he is in need of the grace of God, the giver of wisdom and understanding and insight.
* The weak in the flesh, who being wise in the world forsake their knowledge... become as children of their own free will, and so learn the wisdom that is not acquired by the toil of study.
St. Isaac the Syrian. * God grants wisdom that we may understand it as is fitting.

Theodoret, bishop of Cyrus. * Those who wish to return to their first rank will not be able to do so except by humility. For pride was the cause of the fall at the beginning from heaven. And so whoever lacks deep humility from all his heart and mind and spirit and body does not inherit the kingdom of God.

entries.section: 2. The need for divine wisdom

paragraphs.text: St. Anthony the Great. For though one be perfect among the children of men, yet if thy wisdom be not with him, he shall be counted as nothing. [6]

Solomon realized that the feeling of self-sufficiency and not hungering and thirsting for God deprives man of every divine spiritual gift, even if he appears in the eyes of men successful and good and perfect.

* Everything that a person has through natural creation, when he exercises it, he receives what is through the grace of God. Thus he has an abundance and comes to be in a stronger state in what he has. This is not only with regard to wisdom, but in every good thing we must reflect upon the words of Solomon: "For though a man be perfect among the children of men, and thy wisdom be not with him, he shall be counted as nothing.

Origen. * The man who is wise by the standards of the world is in truth very ignorant, because he does not put away corrupt teaching. A little learning is a dangerous thing, for it makes those who possess it unwilling to learn more. The unlearned are more ready to learn; they are not so ignorant as those who think themselves wise.
St. John Chrysostom

entries.section: 3. Every person has a mission

paragraphs.text: 7 Thou hast chosen me to be a king of thy people, and a judge of thy sons and daughters, 8 and hast commanded me to build a temple upon thy holy mount, and an altar in the city of thy dwelling, a resemblance of the holy tabernacle which thou hast prepared from the beginning.
Thou hast chosen me to be a king of thy people, and a judge of thy sons and daughters. [7]

Solomon prayed and received, for along with his realization of God's surpassing resources, and his need to enjoy God's wisdom and grace, he also realized that he has a special, distinct mission that will not be accomplished by human resources, but by the grace of God ready to work. For besides the general mission to which every man is committed, every person has a special mission, which it befits him to recognize in order to accomplish it according to God's plan and divine good pleasure. So Solomon was set up as king over the people of God for a mission according to God's plan.

entries.section: 3. Every person has a mission

paragraphs.text: And hast commanded me to build a temple upon thy holy mount, and an altar in thy dwelling place, a resemblance of the holy tabernacle, which thou hast prepared from the beginning. [8]

It was not possible for Moses the prophet to set up the tabernacle of the testimony according to his own human thought, but he set it up according to the pattern which the Lord showed him in heaven, that it might be an icon of heaven. For it is said: "Who serve unto the example and shadow of heavenly things, as Moses was admonished of God when he was about to make the tabernacle: for, See, saith he, that thou make all things according to the pattern shewed to thee in the mount" (Heb 8:5).

And now it was not in Solomon's mind to build the holy temple identical to the tent of meeting, but according to the holy tabernacle which God had prepared from the beginning, that is, the one existing in heaven.
This is the mission of every true believer, to set up by the Holy Spirit of God and divine wisdom a temple for the Lord after the likeness of heaven itself. As Holy Scripture says:
"Know ye not that ye are the temple of God, and that the Spirit of God dwelleth in you?" (1 Cor 3:16).
"If any man defile the temple of God, him shall God destroy; for the temple of God is holy, which temple ye are" (1 Cor 3:17).
"What? know ye not that your body is the temple of the Holy Ghost which is in you, which ye have of God, and ye are not your own?" (1 Cor 6:19).

"Him that overcometh will I make a pillar in the temple of my God, and he shall go no more out: and I will write upon him the name of my God, and the name of the city of my God, which is new Jerusalem, which cometh down out of heaven from my God: and I will write upon him my new name" (Rev 3:12).
"He that sitteth on the throne shall dwell among them" (Rev 7:15).

* Everyone whom the Word of God leads to strive together in the way of godliness is a precious stone in the one great temple of God. Therefore Peter the Apostle says: "Ye also, as lively stones, are built up a spiritual house, an holy priesthood, to offer up spiritual sacrifices, acceptable to God by Jesus Christ" (1 Pet 2:5). And Paul the Apostle also says: "And are built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Jesus Christ himself being the chief corner stone" (Eph 2:20). Something similar is also found by a hidden allusion in that passage of Isaiah in which he addresses Jerusalem: "Behold, I will build thy stones with antimony, and lay thy foundations with sapphires, and make thy pinnacles rubies, and thy gates of carbuncle stones, and all thy borders of precious stones, and all thy children shall be taught of the Lord, and great shall be the peace of thy children" (Isa 54:11-14).
So among the righteous there are some who are antimony, and some who are sapphire, and others carbuncle, or precious stones, that is, there are in them all kinds for choosing.
Origen

entries.section: 4. A second cry for wisdom

paragraphs.text: 9 With thee is wisdom, which knoweth thy works, and which was present when thou madest the world, and knoweth what is pleasing in thine eyes, and what is right in thy commandments. 10 O send her out of thy holy heavens, and send her from the throne of thy glory, that being present she may labour with me, and I may know what is pleasing unto thee. 11 For she knoweth and understandeth all things, and she shall be to me a prudent guide in my doings, and preserve me by her glory. 12 So shall my works be acceptable, and I shall judge thy people with justice, and shall be worthy of my father's throne. 13 For what man is he that can know the counsel of God? or who can discern what the Lord willeth? 14 For the thoughts of men are hesitant, and our insights are not firm. 15 For the corruptible body presseth down the soul, and the earthly dwelling weigheth down the mind that is full of cares. 16 And hardly do we picture the things that are upon earth, and with toil do we perceive the things that are before us: but the things that are in the heavens, who hath searched them out?
With thee is wisdom, which knoweth thy works, and was present when thou madest the world, and knoweth what is pleasing in thine eyes, and what is right according to thy commandments. [9]

Solomon the wise looks toward the divine throne and sees the divine hypostasis of wisdom seated upon it, the object of the Father's delight and good pleasure. It is as though he had already heard the voice of the heavenly Father during the baptism of the Lord Christ as well as during His transfiguration: "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased" (Mt 3:17; 17:5; Mk 1:11; Lk 3:22; 2 Pet 1:17).

Solomon realized man's inability to be an object of the Father's delight, after he chose disobedience of his own will, and in pride accepted the counsel of the devil instead of believing the divine promises.
Solomon longed to acquire the divine wisdom and to be hidden in Him, so that through Him he might become an object of the Father's delight, and Solomon himself also take delight in God.

Holy Scripture has expressed the mutual delight between God and man in Jesus Christ the Crucified, who offered reconciliation between the Father and man. For this reason it is often said of the burnt offering, the symbol of the Cross: "it is a burnt offering unto the LORD: it is a sweet savour, an offering made by fire unto the LORD" (Ex 29:18; cf. Ex 29:15, 41; Lev 1:9, 17, etc.). This is about God's delight in us in Christ, the object of His delight. As for our side, it is said: "The fear of the Lord is glory, and boasting, and gladness, and a crown of rejoicing" (Sir 1:11). "The service keeps the heart, and justifies it, and gives gladness and joy" (Sir 1:18).

This is what drove Solomon toward seeking wisdom, since through the hypostasis of wisdom he becomes an object of God's delight, and himself enjoys delight and joy. The son of Sirach says of wisdom: "Whoever loves her loves life, and they that seek to her early shall be filled with joy. He that holdeth her fast shall inherit glory, and wheresoever she entereth, there is the blessing of the Lord" (Sir 4:12-13).
* Make us happy, O my God, in our occupation with You, so that we do not lose You.
* I say, happy is he who possesses God.

entries.section: 4. A second cry for wisdom
