paragraphs.text: St. Augustine. O send her out of thy holy heavens, and send her from the throne of thy glory, that being present she may stand by me and labour with me, and I may know what is pleasing unto thee. [10]

Solomon was longing for the coming of the Lord Christ, the heavenly Word. He asks that the wisdom of God come down from the holy heavens, to carry him to heaven and bestow upon him the holy life. And that He be sent from the throne of glory, to bring him in to the throne.
The wisdom of God came to stand at our side against the devil, and to work in us and by us and with us, and to disclose to us the Father's delight in us.
* James (Jas 1:6) shows that the foundation of all human wisdom is faith. Here he attacks Simon the Magician, who asked the two Apostles to give him the Holy Spirit, and did not ask to receive faith.
Hilary of Arles. * Today "the carpenter's son"... made for Himself a living ladder, setting its base upon the earth, and its head rose toward heaven, and upon it God rests.

It is she whose image Jacob contemplated (Gen 28:12); by her God came down in His steadfastness, or rather bowed down in condescension, and "shewed himself upon earth, and conversed with men" (Bar 3:38).

Father John of Damascus. * How does God take the wise in their own craftiness? (Job 5:13) By showing them, while they think they are able to work without God, that they rather have need of Him. They enter into distress until they show themselves to be less than fishermen and the unlearned, and where they cannot work without their wisdom.

entries.section: 4. A second cry for wisdom

paragraphs.text: St. John Chrysostom. For she knoweth and understandeth all things, and shall lead me wisely in my doings, and preserve me by her glory. [11]

Who knoweth the Father but the Son, and he to whom the Son reveals Him? The Son, "Wisdom," alone is able to disclose to us the divine mysteries, and to give us our understanding, and to take us by the hands to lead us to heavenly glory, keeping us from the evil enemy.
* Spiritual wisdom is the cause of every perfect work. This is the heavenly wisdom, and when we are strengthened by it we can do everything perfectly.

Theophylact. * It is right for us to be there in the presence of God in the heavens, we who kept the lesson while we were on earth, and went there to heaven to be in the love of God the Father, whom we knew while on earth, and because God the Word the Holy One made all things and taught us and teaches us all things, and He trains us in all good things.

entries.section: 4. A second cry for wisdom

paragraphs.text: St. Clement of Alexandria. So shall my works be acceptable, and I shall judge thy people righteously, and shall be worthy of my father's throne. [12]
Without the Lord Christ our works will not be accepted, nor will our mission be accomplished.
* Do you also concede this, that Christ is "the power of God, and the wisdom of God"? You answer: "We concede this."

Listen then: "The spirit of the righteous is the seat of wisdom" (Wis 1). Yes, for what is the seat of God but the place where He dwells? And where does God dwell but in His temple? "For the temple of God is holy, which temple ye are" (1 Cor 3:17).
Be watchful in your reception of God. "God is a Spirit: and they that worship him must worship him in spirit and in truth" (Jn 4:24).
Let the ark of the covenant enter your hearts, and let Dagon fall, if you will" (1 Sam 5:3).
Listen now. And learn to long for God. Be ready to learn how to see God. For He says: "Blessed are the pure in heart: for they shall see God."

entries.section: 4. A second cry for wisdom

paragraphs.text: St. Augustine. For what man is he that can know the counsel of God? or who can conceive what the will of the Lord is? [13]
Our Christ declares in us the divine will, and gives us the ability to carry it out in practice.

* If I am not mistaken, it is not mentioned anywhere that He (Jesus Christ) prayed with His disciples. In every place He prayed alone, because human prayers cannot take hold of the counsels of God (Wis 9:13; Isa 40:13), and no one can share in the inner mysteries of Christ.

entries.section: 4. A second cry for wisdom

paragraphs.text: St. Ambrose. For the thoughts of mortal men are miserable, and our considerations are not firm [14]

Solomon the wise confesses that he is in need of the divine wisdom, who declares the will of the Father and fulfills it in us, and even gives us steadfastness in Him, so that our thoughts are not like a storm at the mercy of the winds, nor our longings and thoughts wavering.

* The psalmist sings: "Come ye unto him, and be enlightened: and your faces shall not be ashamed" (Ps 34:5). We draw near to God by faith, and faith is the work of the spirit and not of the body. But since we do not know what degree of perfection the spiritual body attains, for we are speaking here of a matter in which we have no experience, but on the responsibility of Holy Scripture we do not speak in a definite manner, we must have recourse to the words of the Book of Wisdom: "The thoughts of men are hesitant, and our considerations are not firm" (Wis 9:14).

entries.section: 4. A second cry for wisdom

paragraphs.text: St. Augustine. For the corruptible body presseth down the soul, and the earthly tabernacle weigheth down the mind that is full of cares. [15]

Origen sees that those who love God with all their souls and desire to be united with Him draw themselves away from the weight of the (lusts of the) body and all material things, praying with the Apostle Paul: "O wretched man that I am! who shall deliver me from the body of this death?" (Rom 7:24). They groan in this tabernacle (that of the body), being burdened with the corruptible body (2 Cor 5:4).

* Why then do we hesitate and doubt to put off the corruptible man who hinders us and weighs down the soul, the earthly tabernacle that fills the mind with many cares, so that we may be freed from our bonds, and turn back from the stormy waves that are the lot of flesh and blood? For by this we enjoy Christ Jesus, the rest that accompanies blessedness, and contemplate in Him in His fullness the life-giving Word. And as we feed on Him we perceive the manifold wisdom in Him, and are sealed with the very truth, and our minds are enlightened with the light of true knowledge that does not grow dim, and we enjoy the sight of those things which are seen by the eyes enlightened by the commandment of the Lord (Ps 19:8; Eph 1:18).

Origen. * We were told by the prophet to rend our hearts and not our garments (Joel 2:13), which we can do when we remember that we ourselves often sin at least in thought if not in deed. For the earthly tabernacle represents the mind full of cares (Wis 9:15), and our earth does not cease to produce thorns and thistles for us. We are unable to eat our bread unless we toil with effort and the sweat of our brow.

Father Fulgentius. * Even if our dust is to some extent bound to evil, and the earthly tabernacle presses down upon the soul that flies to the heights (Wis 9:15), which was created to soar on high; yet let the image be washed from defilement and lift up the body that is its partner in the yoke, lifting it up on the two wings of the mind.

St. Gregory of Nazianzus. * We must not ascribe deviation in the wandering of the heart to human nature or to its Creator, for Holy Scripture says truly: "God hath made man upright; but they have sought out many inventions" (Eccl 7:29). The difference of thoughts depends upon ourselves, for good thought draws near to those who know it and the sensible man finds it. So whatever is subject to our discernment and our work we can attain, and if we do not attain it this is due to our laziness and neglect and not to a fault in our nature.

If this matter were not within our power the Lord would not have rebuked the Pharisees, saying: "Wherefore think ye evil in your hearts?" (Mt 9:4). Nor would the prophet have been commissioned to say: "put away the evil of your doings from before mine eyes" (Isa 1:16), "How long shall thy vain thoughts lodge within thee?" (Jer 4:14), nor would the kind of our thoughts have been considered on the Day of Judgment, since God threatens through Isaiah, saying: "And I will recompense their works and their thoughts" (Isa 66:18). It would not be right to recompense or punish according to the testimony of our thoughts in that dreadful and deadly examination, since the blessed Apostle says: "their conscience also bearing witness, and their thoughts the mean while accusing or else excusing one another. In the day when God shall judge the secrets of men according to my gospel" (Rom 2:15-16).

Father Serenus. * Shall we be young or old when we rise? If we die young (as children) and rise young, we shall need nurses in the resurrection. In any case, if we die young and rise old, then the dead do not rise at all; they will be changed into new beings.

Will there be distinction of sex in the world to come? Or will there be no such distinction? If the distinction continues there will be marriage and bodily relations and the begetting of children. If it does not continue, then the bodies that will rise will not be themselves. It is said: "The earthly tabernacle weigheth down the mind that is full of cares" (Wis 9:15). But the bodies that we have in heaven will be refined and spiritual, as the Apostle says: "It is sown a natural body; it is raised a spiritual body" (1 Cor 15:44).

St. Jerome. * Share with me in my labor, for you see what I have undertaken, and who I am who have undertaken it. You see what I desire to speak about, and where and what my condition is except that I am in [the corruptible body that weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling that weighs down the mind full of many cares (cf. Wis 9:15). Therefore I strip my thought of the many things, and gather it in the one God, the indivisible Trinity, so that I may be able to see something to speak about. Let them know that in that [body (which) weighs down the soul] I am able to say "Unto thee, O LORD, do I lift up my soul" (Ps 25:1) LXX (that I may be able to speak to you of things worthy of the subject). May the Lord help me and lift up my soul with me. For I am very weak in relation to Him, and He is very mighty in relation to me."

* (The righteous) who have died have truly been stripped of the corruptible body that weighs down the soul (Wis 9:15). But they still await the redemption of their bodies (Rom 8:23), where their bodies rest in hope (Acts 2:26), but have not yet shone with the incorruption that is to come.
* Let us bear in mind that in this body that weighs down the soul (Wis 9:15) we live a miserable life.

* We are men who carry a body, which walks in this life; and although we have been born again of the seed of the word of God, yet in Christ we have been renewed in such a way that we have still not been completely delivered from Adam. For truly the mortal and corruptible part weighs down the soul (Wis 9:15), showing itself to be present, and declaring that it is from Adam, but what is spiritual in us and raises up the soul is the gift of God and of His mercy, who sent His only-begotten Son to share our death and lead us to His immortality.

* Let us lift up our souls to God, and not against God, for it is said: "Unto thee, O LORD, do I lift up my soul" (Ps 25:1). Let us lift them up with His help, for they are heavy. And what is the cause of their heaviness? Because the corruptible body weighs down the soul (Wis 9:15), and the earthly tabernacle presses upon it, and it is occupied with many things.
* Since we are burdened with such a very heavy load, under which we groan, how shall I lift up my soul unless He lifts it up with me, He who gave Himself for me?

* On one side our corruptible body is a weight upon our souls, and on the other the cause of this hindrance is not in the nature and essence of the body. Therefore, since we know its corruption, we do not desire to be unclothed of the body but rather that it put on its incorruption. In the immortal life we shall have a body, but it will no longer be a weight since it will no longer be corruptible... We have been weighed down, then, by this corruptible body. But since we know that this state of weight is not from the nature and essence of the body but from its corruption, we therefore do not desire to be rid of it but to put it on with its incorruption. Then there will be a body, but it will no longer be a weight because it will no longer be corruptible.
* This body that is dead because of sin lives, which is without doubt corruptible and is a weight upon the soul (Wis 9:13).
* The word "corruptible" was added to show that the soul is weighed down not by any body whatever, but by the body that has come to this state through the fruit of sin.

* If every sin is evil, who can resist? We answer: The nature of man is good and at the same time also able to be freed from evil. For this reason we pray earnestly: "deliver us from evil" (Mt 6:13). This deliverance is not fully accomplished as long as the soul is weighed down by the body that hastens toward corruption (Wis 9:15). In any case, this process is accomplished by grace through faith, so that it is said: [O death, where is thy struggle? O death, where is thy sting? The sting of death is sin; and the strength of sin is the law] (cf. 1 Cor 15:55-56).

* The prayer of the whole City of God, while she is in a state of exile, cries out to God with the mouth of all her members: "Forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors" (Mt 6:12). This prayer is effective not for those who have a dead faith without works (Jas 2:17), but for those whose faith worketh by love (Gal 5:6). For they, though subject to God, are weighed down by the corruptible body (Wis 9:15), so long as it is mortal, and it has not complete authority over vice. For this reason the righteous need this prayer. For although they exercise authority, the vices do not submit without resistance.

St. Augustine. St. Augustine fears that the believer may fall into despair when he is fought with a fleshly lust or a carnal thought that weighs upon the soul, for as long as man is in this world the corruptible body remains resisting, but there is a great difference between resistance and surrender.

* Although every crime is a sin, not every sin is a crime. Thus we say that the life of the saints may be free from crime, but as John the Apostle says: "If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us" (1 Jn 1:8). But even crimes themselves, however great, can be forgiven in the Holy Church, and there is no despair of God's mercy for those who truly repent, each according to the measure of his sin.

entries.section: 4. A second cry for wisdom

paragraphs.text: St. Augustine. And hardly do we guess at things that are upon earth, and with difficulty do we find the things that are before us: but the things that are in the heavens, who can discover? [16]

With difficulty man can come to know some of the secrets of the visible world, and yet he still stands on the shore of the ocean of knowledge, so how can he come to know the secrets of the heavenly God and the heavenly things? Does he not need the divine wisdom to declare by Himself concerning Himself and His Father and His Holy Spirit?

* While the seraphim are not able even to behold God, who does not reveal Himself to them except as a condescension on His part according to their weakness, we see men who dare to picture in their minds the very nature which the seraphim are unable to comprehend. They claim that they are able to look upon it clearly and without limits. Tremble, O heavens, and be astonished, O earth".

* "Truly God is incomprehensible and cannot be approached, even for these orders. For this reason He condescends to appear in the manner recorded in the Revelation. God, who is not bounded by place and does not sit upon a throne... out of His love for us appears seated on a throne with the heavenly powers surrounding Him.

When He appeared on the throne and these powers surrounded Him, these powers could not behold Him nor bear to look at the brightness of His light, so they covered their eyes with their wings, and they had nothing left but to praise and sing with hymns full of glory and holy trembling, and songs bearing witness to the holiness of Him who sits upon the throne."
St. John Chrysostom

entries.section: 5. A third cry

paragraphs.text: 17 And thy counsel who hath known, except thou give wisdom, and send thy Holy Spirit from above? 18 For so the ways of them which are upon the earth were set straight, and men were taught the things that are pleasing unto thee, 19 and by wisdom were saved all that pleased thee, O Lord, from the beginning.
And who hath known thy counsel, except thou give wisdom, and send thy Holy Spirit from on high? [17]
Our Christ, who loved us even unto death so as to save us and bring us into union with Him, offers us on the night of His passion another Comforter, saying:

"But the Comforter, which is the Holy Ghost, whom the Father will send in my name, he shall teach you all things, and bring all things to your remembrance, whatsoever I have said unto you" (Jn 14:16-18, 26).
"But when the Comforter is come, whom I will send unto you from the Father, even the Spirit of truth, which proceedeth from the Father, he shall testify of me" (Jn 15:26).

"Howbeit when he, the Spirit of truth, is come, he will guide you into all truth: for he shall not speak of himself; but whatsoever he shall hear, that shall he speak: and he will shew you things to come. He shall glorify me: for he shall receive of mine, and shall shew it unto you" (Jn 16:13-14).

* A man does not have wisdom and understanding and counsel and fortitude and knowledge and godliness and the fear of God unless he receives the spirit of wisdom and understanding and counsel and fortitude and knowledge and godliness and the fear of God, according to the saying of the Apostle (2 Tim 1:7; Isa 11:2-3).

* This is the wisdom that tames the tongue, descending from above (Jas 3:17), and does not spring from a human heart. Would anyone dare to snatch it away from the grace of God and, in the conceit of pride, put it under the authority of man?
St. Augustine. * Wisdom is given not through a book that one learns, but through the enlightenment of the Holy Spirit.

Father Ambrosiaster. * When the soul is united with the Comforter Spirit in ineffable intimacy, and is wholly mingled with the Spirit, it is counted worthy to become itself spirit, and in its mingling with Him it then becomes wholly light and eye and joy and rest and gladness and love and compassion and goodness and tender mercies.
St. Gregory of Nyssa She entered into the soul of the servant of the Lord, and withstood dreadful kings with wonders and signs. [16]

If the wisdom of God raised up Moses the prophet as a leader for the salvation of his people, then the secret of the power is not in the person of Moses, but in the wisdom of God that entered into his soul because he was the servant of the Lord. The resistance to Pharaoh and the men of his army was not from the human wisdom of Moses, nor his plans, nor his abilities, but it was "the wisdom of God" that repelled the continual assaults.

What happened with Moses the prophet to accomplish the Exodus was a type of the accomplishment of an exodus from the captivity of the devil into the divine embrace. It is a type of what the believers in Christ Jesus, the Savior of the world, enjoy, and of their surpassing victory over the devil and his kingdom.
And the signs and wonders that were accomplished, such as the ten plagues, were the work of the wisdom of God. And the means of enjoying the work of wisdom is faith together with prayer.

The use of the plural indicates the resistance of the kings surrounding them during their wandering in the wilderness, besides the resistance of Pharaoh to them while they were in Egypt and immediately after their departure. Perhaps by the kings he means the rulers of the provinces of Egypt.
* By the Passover these came out of the bondage of Pharaoh, and we, on the day of the crucifixion, are delivered from the bondage of Satan.
They slew a lamb from the flock, and by its blood they were saved from the destroyer, and we were saved by the blood of a chosen Son from the works of corruption that we have done.
They had Moses as a leader, and we have Jesus as a guide and Savior.

Moses divided the sea for them and made them pass through, but our Savior broke open Hades and shattered its gates, and entered within and opened them. And He marked out the way before all who believe in Him.
Moses gave them water from the rock, and our Savior caused living water to flow for us from His breast.
Moses promised them the land of the Canaanites as an inheritance, and our Lord promised us the land of life as a kingdom.

Moses lifted up a serpent of brass; everyone who looked at it remained alive in spite of the bite of the serpent. And Jesus hung Himself up, and everyone who looks to Him is saved from the wound of the serpent, who is Satan.

Moses made for them the temporary tabernacle in which to offer sacrifices and offerings, that they might be cleansed from their sins. And Jesus raised up the tabernacle of David that is fallen down (Amos 9:10; Acts 15:16), and rose. And He said to the Jews: "Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up" (Jn 2:19). And His disciples understood that He spoke of His body, which He raises after three days when they kill Him. For in this tabernacle He promised us life, and by it our sins are cleansed.
He called their tabernacle a temporary tabernacle, because it served for a short time, and He called our tabernacle the temple of the Holy Spirit, which endures forever (1 Cor 3:16; 6:19).
* Moses brought his people out of the service of Pharaoh, and Jesus delivered the nations from the service of Satan.
Moses was brought up in the house of Pharaoh, and Jesus was brought up in Egypt when Joseph fled with Him there.
Miriam stood on the edge of the river when Moses floated on the water, and Mary conceived Jesus when the angel Gabriel gave her the good news.
When Moses slew the lamb, the firstborn of the Egyptians were killed, and Jesus became the true Lamb when they crucified Him, and by His death the murderous people died.
Moses brought down manna for his people, and Jesus gave His body to the nations.
With a tree Moses sweetened the bitter waters, and by His cross Jesus sweetened our bitterness with the wood of the tree of His cross.
Moses brought down the Law for his people, and Jesus gave His covenants to the nations.
Moses conquered Amalek when he stretched out his hands, and Jesus conquered Satan by the sign of the cross.
Moses brought forth waters from the rock for his people, and Jesus sent Simon Cephas to carry His teaching among the nations.
Moses lifted the veil from his face and spoke with God, and Jesus took the veil away from the face of the nations so that they might hear His teaching and receive it.
Moses laid his hand on his apostles and they received the priesthood, and Jesus laid His hand on His apostles and they received the Holy Spirit.
Moses went up the mountain and died there, and Jesus ascended to heaven and sat at the right hand of the Father.

St. Aphrahat the Persian Sage * When Moses saw that all the people (the Egyptians) agreed with their leader (Pharaoh) in his evil, he struck all the Egyptians with a plague, and no one escaped the calamities (Ex 7:17 etc.). And all the elements of the universe - earth, water, air and fire, which enter into everything that exists - cooperated with him in this attack on the Egyptians, as though they were an army carrying out orders, and these elements changed their natural laws to serve human purposes. For at the same time, in the same place and with the same force, sinners were being punished while those who were not sinners suffered nothing.
St. Gregory of Nyssa She rendered to the saints a reward of their labors, and guided them in a wondrous way, and was a shelter to them by day, and a light of stars in the night. [17]

Here he points even to the material recompense, in that they took the precious things belonging to the Egyptians in return for their enslavement and the deprivation of their rights (Ex 3:21-22; 11:2-3; 12:35-36). Perhaps by the recompense he refers to liberation from bondage.

"A shelter by day," for the cloud was a guide to them and at the same time a shelter to protect them from the heat of the sun. "And the LORD will create upon every dwelling place of mount Zion, and upon her assemblies, a cloud and smoke by day, and the shining of a flaming fire by night: for upon all the glory shall be a defence. And there shall be a tabernacle for a shadow in the daytime from the heat, and for a place of refuge, and for a covert from storm and from rain" (Isa 4:5-6).

Here the wise man explained the appearance of the Lord as a cloud shading them by day and a pillar of fire giving them light and leading them, saying that He is wisdom, or the wisdom of God (who later became incarnate to save the world).

* The divine power sent a cloud to lead the people (Ex 13:21-22), and this was not an ordinary cloud, for it was not composed of vapors like ordinary clouds, nor was it a misty formation produced by the pressure of the winds on vapors, but it was something beyond human understanding. And Scripture bears witness that there was something extraordinary in this cloud, for when the rays of the noonday sun shone with intense heat, the cloud was a shelter for the people, casting shade from above and moistening the fiery heat of the air with a light dew. And during the night it was changed into fire leading the Israelites - as in a procession - with its light from sunset to sunrise.
St. Gregory of Nyssa She brought them through the Red Sea, and led them through much water. [18]

The way that wisdom chose for the departure from Egypt and the crossing to the land of promise was to bring them through the Red Sea and make them pass through much water. This was not the way according to human logic, since there was an easy and smooth road at that time, the one in the direction of El-Arish, by which they would reach the Jordan directly. No one realized the mystery in this, since it was not possible for them to enter the land of promise except through this way, for the following reasons: 1. The crossing of the Red Sea as a type of the enjoyment of Baptism, so that the believers may cross over to the heavenly Canaan. 2. Entering into tribulations and wars, so that Pharaoh and his soldiers perish as a sign of the destruction of the devil and his angels. And Amalek and other nations are defeated, as they are types of the sins that he must crush by the power of the cross during our striving by the grace of God. 3. The people's remaining forty years so that they might completely forget every experience of idolatry with which they had come into contact in Egypt. 4. So that Moses might die and Joshua take over the leadership, for there is no entering into eternity unless the letter of the Law dies and we live by the Spirit under the leadership of our Lord Jesus (Joshua). 5. The enjoyment of the experience of praise in the midst of the wilderness. 6. The enjoyment of the heavenly manna as a type of partaking of the Body and Blood of the Lord. 7. The enjoyment of taking refuge under the wings of the Lord (the cloud) and of being enlightened by His Holy Spirit (the pillar of fire by night).

* In that crossing the pillar of cloud was a guide. And those before us did well in interpreting the pillar of cloud as the mercy of the Holy Spirit, who guides those worthy toward the good; and whoever follows the Holy Spirit crosses the waters, since the guide makes a way for him in them, and in this way leads him safely to freedom, but the one who pursues him to bring him back to bondage perishes in the water. Those who hear this must not be ignorant of the mystery of the water. For whoever goes down into the water with the enemy's army comes out alone, leaving the enemy's army to drown in the water.
St. Gregory of Nyssa But their enemies she drowned, and then cast them up from the bottom of the deep. [19]

* Moses himself watched the cloud and taught the people how it remained within their sight (Ex 14:16-22). And after the cloud had guided them along their whole course, they reached the Red Sea, where the Egyptians, coming up from behind, surrounded the people with all their army. And there was no escape from this terror available to the Israelites in any direction, for they were hemmed in between their enemies and the water. Then Moses - moved by a divine power - carried out the most marvelous deed, scarcely to be believed at all: he approached the shore and struck the sea with his rod. And the sea was split by the blow, just as a crack that occurs in glass runs from any point to the edge. In this way the whole sea was split from above by the action of the rod, and the cleft ran through the waters until it reached the opposite shore. And in the place where the sea was split, Moses went down into the depth with all the people without being wetted, and their bodies were still bathed in the light of the sun. And while they were crossing the depths on foot over the dry bottom, they were not troubled by the sight of the water rising so near them on both sides, for the sea had been fixed like a wall on both sides.

And when Pharaoh and the Egyptians pursued them and went down after them into the sea, in the newly split passage, the walls of water joined together again, and the sea rushed to take its former shape, and became one mass of water (Ex 14:23-31). At that time the Israelites had reached the other bank after the long and wearisome walk in the sea, and then they sang the song of victory to God, who had done a great deed without any shedding of blood on their part, for He destroyed the whole army of the Egyptians in the water, all the horses and the foot soldiers and the chariots.

* Who is there who does not know that the Egyptian army, with its horses and chariots and their drivers and its slingers (with slings and bows) and its soldiers armed with heavy weapons and the rest of the enemy's forces in the battle line, are a type of the various passions of the soul that enslave man? For the intellectual impulses and the unrestrained sensual inclinations toward pleasure and pain and greed are exactly like the army we have mentioned. And abuse and insult are like the stones that are hurled with slings, and recklessness is the point of the brandished spear. As for the love of pleasure, it is represented by the horses that draw the chariot with an irresistible impulse.

We read in the history in the book of Exodus that the chariot had three men on it who drove it, called "captains," and since you have already learned the mystery of the doorposts and the upper lintel, you understand that these three whom the chariot carries correspond to the threefold division of the soul: the rational, the emotional and the spiritual.

The whole army rushes into the water after the Israelites, who went before them in the crossing that was deadly (for the army). Then we find the rod of faith leading the way, and the pillar of cloud giving light, and giving water and life to those who find refuge in it, and destroying their pursuers.

The history (the Scripture) teaches us here what kind of people will cross the water and not take with them any of the enemy's army as they come out of the water. For if the enemy came out with them from the water, they would continue in bondage after their coming out, since they would have brought the tyrant with them alive and not drowned him in the water. And if someone wishes to make clear the type in this picture, it is evident that those who pass through the water of holy Baptism must kill the whole army of evil, this army which includes greed and unrestrained desires and thoughts of covetousness and passions of conceit and arrogance, and recklessness, anger, spite and envy and all these things. And since the passions by nature follow our nature, we must kill in the water the base inclinations of the mind and the works that result from them.
St. Gregory of Nyssa And therefore the righteous spoiled the ungodly, and praised Your holy name, O Lord.
And they praised with one accord Your hand that defended them. [20]

The book of Exodus does not mention the fate of Pharaoh's army after it was drowned in the sea. Here he mentions that the corpses, after they sank to the depths, floated above the waters, and the Israelites stripped what was on the dead bodies.
This tradition is found in Josephus, namely the Hebrews' taking what the Egyptians who died by drowning in the Red Sea possessed, a matter which is not mentioned in the book of Exodus.

* When Pharaoh and the Egyptians pursued them and went down after them into the sea, in the newly split passage, the walls of water joined together again, and the sea rushed to take its former shape, and became one mass of water (Ex 14:23-31). At that time the Israelites had reached the other bank after the long and wearisome walk in the sea, and then they sang the song of victory to God, who had done a great deed without any shedding of blood on their part, for He destroyed the whole army of the Egyptians in the water, all the horses and the foot soldiers and the chariots.
St. Gregory of Nyssa For wisdom opened the mouth of the dumb, and made the tongues of infants plain. [21]

It is said in the Targum that some of the children of the Hebrews who were threatened with death in Egypt were carried by angels to the wilderness, and later took part in the journey in the wilderness.
Perhaps the children joined the people in the praise (Ex 15).
Your love is surpassing, O You who watch over Your people!
* You created everything to prepare the palace for Adam my father; You brought him to the garden of Eden as to a royal palace.
You loved him and gave him all authority.
And when he fell You did not forsake him.
You gave him the promise of salvation.
You came for his sake and for the sake of his children, and carried the cross of shame for their salvation.
Glory to You, O second Adam, Father of mankind!
* You sent fire that consumed the sacrifice of Abel; You breathed it in as a sweet savor of pleasure and acceptance.
But his wretched brother withdrew from You.
So anger ruled over him, and he killed his brother!
Grant me not to withdraw my hand from Your hand.
Nor to shut the door of my heart before You.
So that I may love my brethren, even those who oppose me.
* The smell of corruption and abominations spread in the world.
And there was no longer any hope of reform, for mankind was treating its Creator with contempt.
You looked down from heaven and embraced Noah the righteous.
You prepared an ark for him, and You Yourself shut him in.
In the midst of the flood Noah was kept in Your heart.
In the midst of the total destruction, the ark was an object of admiration to the heavenly ones.
Carry me in Your cross, the ark of salvation, for none can rescue me except Your cross, which brings me into the Church, Your holy ship!
* The people turned their backs to You; instead of divine wisdom they sought human cunning.
They resolved to build a tower whose top would be in heaven, to protect them from a coming, destructive flood!
What folly! They were scattered and dispersed.
Instead of their rising up to the heavenly, they became warring nations without peace!
* In the midst of the whole world Abraham, Your friend, was found.
He loved You and possessed You.
With joy he wished to offer his only son as a burnt offering.
So You raised up from his son a people for Yourself.
And You became incarnate of the Virgin Mary, who was of his seed.
Glory to You, in whom all the nations are blessed.
* In the midst of corrupt Sodom lived Lot and his family.
The righteous man tormented his soul with their lawless deeds.
He possessed You, so he could not share with them in their evils.
And when You brought him out of it and sent down fire upon it, he never thought of looking at it, not even out of curiosity.
He lived among them with his heart in isolation from their corruption; how then, after his coming out, would he look at them?
His wife deprived herself of You.
Her heart returned to Sodom, and she looked behind.
She lost all feeling, and became a pillar of salt.
She became a statue bearing witness to every soul that is deprived of union with You!
In her folly she herself became a testimony to folly and ignorance!
* Our father Jacob possessed You and leaned on You.
In the midst of his bitter afflictions he found You the cornerstone; he laid his head upon You, and his insight was opened.
He saw Your cross as a ladder by which he ascends to heaven.
By You the wilderness was turned for him into an open heaven.
His brother hated him, so he beheld angels descending to him, accompanying him.
And he saw angels ascending with him that he might enjoy You.
The bitterness of his soul was turned into surpassing sweetness.
* Laban, his uncle and father-in-law, did not possess You, so he set in his heart to take vengeance on Jacob.
Instead of the spirit of vengeance, You made of him a witness to Your love and Your work with Jacob!
You did not command him to return with his men to where he had been, but You commanded him to meet Jacob, and to bear witness to You that You shepherd him and keep him.
How wonderful, for You turn opponents into witnesses to Your love.
* You turned Joseph's fetters in the prison into a way of passing over to the throne.
The prisoner became the second man in the kingdom.
The chief of police stood in amazement.
The one who brought him into the prison now asks him for bread for himself and for his household.
She who wanted to satisfy the lusts of her body brought him into prison.
Now behold, her body needs bread; who will give it to her but he?
You made the prisoner a source of satisfaction for all Egypt and for the lands surrounding it.
He became a type of You, O Satisfier of souls.
You shone upon him that he might perceive Your eternal glory.
* You heard the groaning of Your people, and Your bowels yearned over them.
You sent them a leader, You kept him for them in the very palace of Pharaoh, You granted that You would speak by his mouth, and You gave him to work wonders and dazzling signs.
* You shepherded Your people Yourself.
You shaded them like a cloud by day, and You were a leader to them like a pillar of fire by night. * You brought them through the midst of the sea, and made them pass in a unique procession.
But those who rejected You, the way became a tomb for them.
They rejected You, O Life, and death swallowed them up.
* You turned Your people into a choir of angels.
They praise You in the midst of the wilderness, and rejoice because of the abundance of Your love!

entries.section: 1. Raising up a leader

paragraphs.text: 1 Then she prospered their works by the hand of a holy prophet. 2 They journeyed through a wilderness that was uninhabited, and pitched their tents in a desolate land, 3 and they withstood those who fought against them, and repelled their enemies.
And she made their endeavors prosper by the hand of a holy prophet. [1]

After speaking of the work of wisdom in the life of the early Fathers, he now records for us her work with the people under the leadership of Moses, "a holy prophet," the leader of the march of the Exodus. As it was said of him: "If there be a prophet among you, I the LORD will make myself known unto him in a vision, and will speak unto him in a dream. My servant Moses is not so, who is faithful in all mine house. With him will I speak mouth to mouth, even apparently, and not in dark speeches; and the similitude of the LORD shall he behold" (Num 12:6-8).
Just as he avoided mentioning the names of the righteous before, here too he avoided the name of Moses the holy prophet.

In every age God sends leaders whose hearts are aflame with the Spirit, who work continually for the sake of the Kingdom of God. God chooses the suitable leader for every age, and equips him with qualities and abilities that suit the circumstances of the age. So He sent Moses to lead the people on the journey of the Exodus. And God prepared Joshua as a type of Jesus Christ, to bring them into the land of promise, and raised up David to repair what Saul had spoiled, and prepared Solomon for the building of the temple, and sent St. Athanasius to resist Arius, and St. Cyril the Great to resist Nestorius.

* After Moses was given authority from the Theophany (the vision of God) that appeared to him, he received a command to deliver his Hebrew countrymen from the bondage of the Egyptians. And in order to be more fully assured of the power God had placed in him, he tested the divine command by the things in his hands (Ex 4:1-7), for when the rod fell from his hand, life stirred in it, and when he took hold of it with his hand again, it returned to what it had been. And when he drew his hand out of his bosom, it became leprous as snow, and when he put it a second time into his bosom, it returned to its natural color.

* After Moses gained strength from the light that was revealed to him, and his brother came as an ally and supporter to him, he boldly proclaimed to the people the good news of freedom, and reminded them of the greatness of their fathers. And he expressed his opinion about the way in which they could be delivered from the hard labor of making bricks (Ex 6).

entries.section: What do we learn from this?

paragraphs.text: We must learn that whoever has not prepared himself by this kind of spiritual training to teach the multitudes should not speak to the people. For we see that when Moses was still young and had not yet matured and reached a high degree of virtue, the two men who were quarreling paid no heed to his sound advice and did not accept it. Yet after his descent from the mountain he addressed tens of thousands in the same manner.

The history of Moses shows us clearly that we must not dare to give advice to those who listen to us in our teaching of them unless the ability for it has been perfected in us by long and arduous training, as it was with Moses.

entries.section: What do we learn from this?

paragraphs.text: St. Gregory of Nyssa So they journeyed through an uninhabited wilderness, and pitched their tents in places that no foot had trodden. [2]

The true leader of the journey of the Exodus was the wisdom of God, for neither the people nor the leader had previous experience in the journey of a people through a desolate wilderness, so there were no guarantees, on a fearful, empty road with no trace of life.
They faced on their journey mighty enemies such as Amalek and others, and they were not men of war, nor did they have weapons, so the victory came as a divine gift presented to them.
He also avoided mentioning certain names such as Aaron and Miriam and others, for what the wisdom of God offered was for the whole congregation if it is sanctified in the Lord.

entries.section: What do we learn from this?

paragraphs.text: And they withstood those who fought against them, and repelled their enemies. [3]

There is no point of comparison between a people that lived in bondage, that had never practiced military life, and had no weapons, and strong enemies experienced in fighting. But the wisdom of God, or the Word of God, was the hidden leader, the giver of victory.

entries.section: 2. The first contrast: water for death in Egypt and another for life in the wilderness

paragraphs.text: 4 And in their thirst they called upon You; and water was given them out of flinty rock, and a quenching of their thirst from the hard stone. 5 So that by which their enemies were tormented, when they lacked what to drink, while the children of Israel rejoiced in its abundance, 6 was the very thing by which kindness was shown them in their need. 7 For You confounded those, in that You changed for them the perennial fountain of the river into foul blood, 8 as a punishment for their decreeing the killing of infants, and to these You gave abundant water when they had despaired of it, 9 that You might show them by this thirst of theirs how You punished their adversaries.
When they thirsted they called upon You, and water was given them out of flinty rock, and a quenching of their thirst from the hard stone. [4]

The water was spent from their vessels in the midst of a barren desert, these who had lived all their days relying on the waters of the Nile, and by human reasoning there was no way of life; but the wisdom of God worked, and a spring of water bursting forth from a hard rock that accompanied them was granted to them (Ex 17:1-7; Num 20:2-13), without human effort. For He did not require them to dig wells from which to drink. This free gift is beyond price, for it is a matter of life or death; a matter of the existence of the people or their destruction. Therefore this rock became a type of the Lord Christ, the Giver of resurrection. "And did all drink the same spiritual drink: for they drank of that spiritual Rock that followed them: and that Rock was Christ" (1 Cor 10:4).

Since the writer wants us to thirst for the water of life, and so to drink from the springs of the love of the Lord Christ, the wisdom of God, he fixed our eyes on the people's recourse to God that they might be refreshed, and did not point to their murmuring (Ex 17:2-3), and that they almost stoned Moses.
What occupies the writer is not the historical presentation of events, but fixing our eyes on the wisdom of God so that we may not lack anything.

The Evangelist describes for us the Lord Christ's call to all mankind to come to Him and drink, as he says: "Jesus stood and cried, saying, If any man thirst, let him come unto me, and drink. He that believeth on me, as the scripture hath said, out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water. But this spake he of the Spirit, which they that believe on him should receive" (Jn 7:37-39). By saying "if any man thirst" He opens the door for all, to come and drink.

entries.section: 2. The first contrast: water for death in Egypt and another for life in the wilderness

paragraphs.text: For the things by which their enemies were punished became those by which kindness was shown to them in their distress. [5]

God punished the unbelieving Egyptians with the waters that were polluted with blood (Ex 7:24), and saved His people with pure waters bursting forth from the rock in the wilderness. The Nile, which is counted a source of life, became a source of death, and the wilderness, which is counted a cause of destruction, offered life. The water became a punishment for those who rejected the wisdom of God, and a blessing for those who enjoy wisdom. So what was a punishment for their enemies became for His people a sign of God's care for them and His concern for them, for He gave them water, not from the river Nile, but from a solid rock.
We can also say that in the waters of Baptism the devil, the enemy of good, loses his authority and his kingdom is shattered, and in the very same waters the baptized enjoys sonship to God.

* At the command of Moses all the waters in Egypt were turned into blood (Ex 7:20-22), and the fish died on account of the thickening of the waters, but for the Hebrews the water remained as it was. And the magicians seized the opportunity to use their art to make the water that had not turned into blood, which was with the Hebrews, appear as though it were blood.

* Whoever possesses the rod of virtue that is not defeated, which swallows up the rod of the magicians, advances to training in greater wonders. And the wonders do not happen to terrify those present, but for the benefit of those who are being rescued. For through the wonders of virtue the enemy is defeated and the people are strengthened.

If we first know the general spiritual purpose of the wonders of virtue, we can then apply this understanding to each miracle in itself. And true faith agrees with the inclinations of those who hear the word; for although the word shows everyone what is good and what is evil, yet the person with good inclinations toward what he hears has his understanding enlightened, while the words of ignorance remain overshadowing the person of stubborn inclinations, who does not allow his spirit to see the ray of truth. And if our general understanding of these matters is not mistaken, then each matter in itself will not appear different, since the part is shown and made clear by the whole.

Therefore it is not at all strange that the Hebrew, though living in the midst of strangers, is not affected by the evil of the Egyptians. We can see the same thing happening now in cities crowded with people whose opinions contradict one another. For some, the river of faith from which they drink through the divine teaching is sweet and pure, while for others who live like the Egyptians and drink with their evil passions, the water becomes for them foul blood.

And many times the master of evil and deceit tries to turn the water of the Hebrews also into blood by corrupting it with fraud and falsehood, that is, by showing us our doctrine otherwise than as it truly is; but he cannot corrupt the water so completely that it is not fit for use at all, even if he easily turned it red by his deceit, for the Hebrew, who pays no heed to the optical illusion, drinks the real water, even if his adversaries succeed in misleading him.

* Once again the cloud rose and led them to another place (Ex 17:1-7). But this place was a barren desert with burning sands, and there was not a drop of water in it. And here again thirst wearied the people. But when Moses struck a projecting rock with his rod, it brought forth sweet water, fit to drink, in greater abundance than all this great multitude needed.

entries.section: 2. The first contrast: water for death in Egypt and another for life in the wilderness

paragraphs.text: St. Gregory of Nyssa And instead of the fountain of a perennial river, troubled with corrupt blood. [6]

God gave them a river with its sweet waters, but by their corruption its water became corrupt, and became a source of destruction to them, not a source of life. So God gave us His commandment as a sweet yoke, but by the evil of our will the yoke becomes heavy, and the good commandment turns into a cause of our condemnation and our destruction.

* How then does the wonderful sweetness of the yoke of Christ become bitter except because of the bitterness of our evil? How does the very light divine burden become heavy, except that in our stubborn insolence we despise the Lord by whom we bear His burden, especially since Scripture itself clearly bears witness to this, saying: "His own iniquities shall take the wicked himself, and he shall be holden with the cords of his sins" (Prov 22:5; Wis 11:16)?

I say it is clear that we are the ones who make the easy, sound ways of the Lord into wearisome ways, because of the heavy stones of our evil lusts, for in folly we make the royal road a stony ground, and we leave the road that the feet of all the saints have trodden, indeed in which the Lord Himself walked, seeking a road with no footprints of those who went before us, seeking places full of thorns, so the allurements of present delights blind us, and the wedding garment is torn by the thorns in the darkness... And the road has been covered with rods of sins, so that we are not only torn by the sharp thorns of the bramble, but are cast down by the bites of deadly serpents and of vipers lurking there, for "thorns and snares are in the way of the froward" (Prov 5:22).

The Lord says in another place through the prophet: "Because my people hath forgotten me... and they have caused them to stumble in their ways from the ancient paths, to walk in paths, in a way not cast up" (Jer 15:18). And Solomon says: "The way of the slothful man is as an hedge of thorns" (Prov 19:15). So when they go astray from the heavenly royal road, they are unable to reach the city on which our gaze was fixed. And the book of Ecclesiastes expressed it symbolically, saying of it that it is Jerusalem... (Eccl 15:10). That is, "Jerusalem which is above is free, which is the mother of us all" (Gal 26:4).

But whoever truly leaves this world and takes the yoke of Christ and learns from Him, and trains himself daily to bear toil, because the Lord is "meek and lowly in heart" (Mt 29:11), remains continually undisturbed by all trials, and for him "all things work together for good" (Rom 28:8). As the prophet (Micah) says, the words of God are good to him who walks uprightly (Mic 2:7).

entries.section: 2. The first contrast: water for death in Egypt and another for life in the wilderness

paragraphs.text: Father Abraham As a punishment for a command to kill infants, You gave them unexpectedly abundant water. [7]

The water flowing in the river Nile became a punishment for the Egyptians, for it became blood (Ex 7:17-21), because they shed the blood of many infants by the command of Pharaoh (Ex 1:8-10), so death threatened the Egyptians.

It is said in Exodus 7:14-24 that this plague came to urge Pharaoh to let the people of God go, but here he sees in this plague a chastisement for Pharaoh's decision to kill the infants of the Hebrews (Ex 1:16, 22). This plague can serve both purposes together.

* In the water the Egyptians used to kill the infants of the children of Israel, and by the water God began their torment, when He made it blood that they could not drink. He measured to them with the measure by which they had measured to others.

St. Mar Ephrem the Syrian * In fact the turning of the water of the river into blood was fitting. The river in which the infants of the Hebrews were cruelly drowned gave back to the perpetrators of that crime a cup of blood, and when they drank from it they were slain by the corrupt waters that they had defiled by wicked murder.

entries.section: 2. The first contrast: water for death in Egypt and another for life in the wilderness

paragraphs.text: Father Caesarius, Bishop of Arles After You had shown them by their thirst at that time how You punished their adversaries. [8]

If God allowed this plague for the Egyptians who resisted the truth, He also allowed the Hebrews to thirst in the midst of the wilderness so that they might experience for a while the bitterness of the plague that struck the Egyptians in depriving them of the pure water of the Nile, so that it might be a lesson for them in the midst of the wilderness.

entries.section: 2. The first contrast: water for death in Egypt and another for life in the wilderness

paragraphs.text: For when they were tested, though it was a chastisement of mercy, they learned how the wicked were tormented, who were judged in wrath. [9]
God's chastening of His people is an instructive work full of mercy.

With God there is no partiality toward the Jews; He chastened the unbelieving Egyptians with the plague of the water that became blood, and the plagues followed one after another, revealing the hardness of their hearts and their insistence on not believing in God the Worker of wonders. As for the Jews, He allowed them the trial of thirst in order to chasten them in His mercy, and when Moses had recourse to God, He gave him water from the rock of Horeb.

entries.section: 3. God the Father and the Ruler!

paragraphs.text: 10 For when they were tested by You, though it was a chastisement of mercy, they understood how the torment of the hypocrites, who were condemned in wrath, had been. 11 For You tried these as a father, admonishing them, and those You tested as a stern king, condemning them. 12 And the same distress touched them in absence as in presence, 13 for a twofold grief seized them, and groaning at the remembrance of past plagues, 14 for when they heard that what was a punishment to them had become kindness to their enemies, they felt the hand of the Lord. 15 And him whom they had before decreed to be cast into the river, and had despised and rejected, they marveled at in the end of the matter, for the thirst of the righteous was unlike their thirst.
For You tested these as a father admonishing them, and those You judged as a stern king condemning them. [10]
What befell the Egyptians was a punishment for restraint, while the thirst that befell the Hebrews was a fatherly chastisement for warning.

entries.section: 3. God the Father and the Ruler!

paragraphs.text: And whether they were absent or present, they suffered torment alike. [11]
Both parties suffered torment alike; thirst befell both parties, but the situation in each case was different from the other.

entries.section: 3. God the Father and the Ruler!

paragraphs.text: For a twofold grief seized them, and groaning at the remembrance of the past. [12]

In the presence of the Jews grief befell the Egyptians when the water turned into blood, and after the Jews departed to the wilderness their grief was doubled, for they saw those whom they had formerly enslaved having become a great people bearing surpassing power, overcoming the difficulties of the wilderness by the God of the impossible, who is able to provide them water from a solid rock that followed them on their journey.

Some see that the grief of the wicked is doubled: grief because of the chastisement that comes upon them, and another grief because of the blessings that are granted to those who trouble them and wrong them.

entries.section: 3. God the Father and the Ruler!

paragraphs.text: For when they heard that what was a punishment for them was a kindness to their enemies, they felt the hand of the Lord. [13]

entries.section: 3. God the Father and the Ruler!

paragraphs.text: For him whom they had cast out before, and rejected with mockery, they marveled at in the end of the matter, for their thirst was unlike the thirst of the righteous. [14]

It seems that all the nations surrounding the region - including Egypt - were following the events of the Exodus. So when the Egyptians heard of the thirst of the Hebrews and then of the bringing forth of water from the rock, they were amazed, and realized that they had previously mocked God through His people and rejected Him, which had destroyed their king and their army, while the Hebrews benefited from the thirst!
Moses the prophet, whom the Egyptians rejected and the Jews also, became the object of amazement to both.
Moses was an instrument that God used for the thirst of the Egyptians, and he himself became an instrument for quenching the thirst of the Israelites.

entries.section: 4. God's forbearance in His dealing with Egypt

paragraphs.text: 16 And since they had been foolish in their wicked thoughts, and went astray so as to worship contemptible creeping things and beasts without speech, You took vengeance on them by sending upon them a multitude of creatures without speech, in return for the foolish, unjust thoughts which led them astray so that they worshiped serpents without speech and contemptible insects, You punished them by sending upon them a multitude of creatures without speech. [15]

Some forms of worship spread in ancient Egypt, such as the worship of the crocodile and the snakes and the fox and the ram (the god Amun), and the Apis bull and the lioness and the cow (the god Hathor) and the falcon, the ape, the hippopotamus, the cat, the frog and the serpent, as well as the beetle and the scarab (among insects).
As for the contemptible insect, perhaps what is meant is the scarab, which the ancient Egyptians exalted, so they engraved it on their rings and their ornaments and their gold.

The chastisement came from the same deed, for since they worshiped animals and reptiles and insects as gods, He struck them with insects and frogs that attacked their houses and entered into their chambers, and many of them died and stank, so they were asking to be rid of them (Ex 8:8).
The Egyptians were struck with three small animals or insects in the plagues 2, 3 and 4, which are the plagues of the frogs, the gnats and the flies.

As for the frogs: St. Augustine sees that they refer to those who speak much that is vain and unprofitable, and Origen sees that they refer to the songs of the poets, which are like the croaking of frogs, producing twisted, annoying sounds without work. And Isidore of Seville (died in the year 636) took this from him, as he says: [In the second plague the frogs were brought. And it is thought that they symbolize the songs of the poets who brought into this world flimsy, deceitful stories. By their empty songs full of vanity, like the croaking of frogs. For the frog produces empty chatter. This animal is of no use at all, but only produces annoying, loathsome sounds.]

And as for the gnats: the priests of the Egyptians were very careful about cleanliness and guarded against being defiled by gnats and lice. Origen sees that the gnats refer to sweetened words that deceive a person with cunning, so that he does not feel them during their deceiving, like gnats that sting and the person does not feel them except after the sting. Therefore Father Isidore of Seville sees that they refer to the heretics.

And as for the flies, God allowed them to reveal the helplessness of the gods of the Egyptians, since they believed that they drove away the flies. And Father Isidore says that the fly is an insolent insect that never rests, and God allowed the Egyptians to be struck with flies that they might realize that their world-loving hearts are struck with the disturbance of passions that never cease.

entries.section: 5. The second contrast: quails in the wilderness against the plague of insects.

paragraphs.text: 17 That they might know that by what things a man sins, by the same he is punished. 18 For it was not difficult for Your hand, which is almighty, which made the world out of formless matter, to send upon them a multitude of bears or bold lions, 19 or new kinds of unknown ravenous beasts, breathing out fire, or sending forth a dark smoke, or flashing dreadful sparks from their eyes. 20 Then they would have destroyed them by fear at their appearance, let alone crushing them by their attack. 21 Yea, a breath was enough to cast them down; justice would pursue them, and the spirit of Your power scatter them. But You have ordered all things in measure and number and weight.
That they might know that every one is punished by that by which he sinned. [16]

The insects came upon the Egyptians in return for their worship of animals such as the crocodile, the snake, the lizard and the frog. For this they were struck with the frogs (Ex 8:1-15), the gnats (Ex 8:16-19), the flies (Ex 8:20-24), and the locusts (Ex 10:3-15).

He links the vain gods, their worshipers and their chastisements. For since they were foolish - without reason - they worshiped irrational animals, and fell under chastisement by irrational animals or insects. So worshipers share with their gods in their characteristics. Whoever worships vain gods becomes vain himself, and whoever worships the Lover of mankind and its Savior becomes a lover of men, and desires to be given for the sake of everyone.

In this passage the writer affirms that the punishment (or chastisement) comes upon the wicked by the very things by which he sinned. For since the Egyptians worshiped animals instead of God, the plagues came upon them by animals and insects.

* It is not easy to decide whether we should despise the worshipers of them or the things that are the object of worship. The more likely is the worshipers, for they are more trivial, because they are of a rational nature and received grace from God, yet they set up the worse instead of the better. And this is the deceit of the evil one, who corrupted what is good to be used for an evil purpose, and that in most of his evil works.
St. Gregory of Nazianzus And it was not hard for Your all-powerful hand, which made the world out of formless matter, to send upon them a multitude of bears, or bold lions. [17]

It is God's care even for the wicked, for He could have destroyed the Egyptians at once by sending upon them bears and lions that devour them, but He sent small insects that trouble them without killing them, in order to chasten them. He did not desire their destruction and death, but seeks their repentance and their life.
The Creator of the world out of an empty and void earth (Gen 1:2) is able to punish by sending ravenous and terrifying beasts, as happened in Samaria (2 Kgs 17:26).
* Although He created things out of things, as He created man from the dust, yet the earth from which the dust came He created out of nothing.

entries.section: 5. The second contrast: quails in the wilderness against the plague of insects.

paragraphs.text: St. Augustine Or ravenous beasts unknown and newly created, full of wrath, either breathing out a fiery blast or belching forth a foul smoke, or sending forth dreadful sparks from their eyes. [18]

Again he says that there was no need to send fierce, savage animals to devour them, nor to create new terrifying animals that destroy them by their frightening sight, but one breath is enough, and all fall and do not rise.

In His justice He could have pursued them with a breath from His mouth; He says a word that issues a sentence of death upon them and they die. But God does not desire to destroy, but to chasten in due measure.

entries.section: 5. The second contrast: quails in the wilderness against the plague of insects.

paragraphs.text: Then they would have destroyed them by fear at their appearance, let alone crushing them by their harm. [19]
Even without these animals, one breath was enough to cast them down, justice pursuing them and scattering them by the breath of Your power.

entries.section: 5. The second contrast: quails in the wilderness against the plague of insects.

paragraphs.text: But You have ordered all things in measure and number and weight. [20]

God the Creator was able to create new beasts that would destroy them, not only by devouring them, but also by the terror that comes upon them from their sight, as it is said of Medusa, who used to destroy people by her terrifying appearance. For even in His chastening of the wicked He does so with wisdom, in measure and number and weight, that is, by an exact divine ordering, and for a purpose in God's mind toward them, without compelling them to return to Him by force.
God is a God of order, not of confusion (1 Cor 14:33); all that He does is with exactness and surpassing divine ordering.

* Every creature, great or small, was made by Him. In Him were created things above and things below, spiritual and material. So there is no form, nor arrangement of parts, nor any matter whatever, of whatever weight or number or measure, that exists except by that Word the Creator, to whom it was said: "You have ordered all things in measure and number and weight" (Wis 11:20).

* In the books of our Scripture it is said to God: "You have ordered all things in measure and number and weight" (Wis 11:21). The prophet also says: "He calleth them all (the host of heaven) by names" (Isa 40:26). And the Savior says in the Gospel: "But the very hairs of your head are all numbered" (Mt 10:30).

* We do not know the number of the saints or the number of the demons, but we know that the children of the holy mother who was called barren on earth (the Church) will occupy the place of the fallen angels, and will dwell forever in that abode full of peace from which they fell. As for the number of the citizens, whether at present or as it will be, it is present in the thoughts of the great Creator, He who called things that are not into being (Rom 4:7), and orders all things by measure and number and weight (Wis 11:20).

St. Augustine St. Augustine also sees that if God in His unlimited knowledge orders everything by a certain number that He knows perfectly, then it is fitting for us to pay attention to the numbers mentioned in Holy Scripture, and to know their symbolic spiritual meanings.

St. Augustine sees that man in his spiritual life may walk in a particular order, through four stages that correspond to the four stages of the history of the Church. In the first stage man is like one in the depth of ignorance, not knowing what he is; the second stage is when he knows sin through the Law, so he feels that he is overcome by sin and a slave to it (Rom 5:5), and as the Apostle says, the Law entered that the offence might abound (Rom 5:20). And when God grants him faith he receives the power of love, so he struggles against the lusts of the flesh, and lives righteous by faith, and is counted righteous as long as he does not submit to evil desire, but overcomes it by his love of holiness. This is the third stage, of good hope. Whoever holds fast to this finally receives in the fourth stage peace, especially at the end when the body rises glorified. These four stages correspond to the stages of the history of the Church. The first stage is before the Law, the second under the Law, the third in the age of grace when the Savior came, and then the fourth in the resurrection.

entries.section: 6. Beyond God's forbearance

paragraphs.text: 22 And You have great power at all times; who can resist the strength of Your arm? 23 For the whole world before You is as what tips the balance of the scales, and as a drop of dew that falls upon the earth at dawn. 24 But You have mercy on all, because You are able to do all things, and You overlook the sins of men that they may repent. 25 For You love all existing things, and loathe nothing that You made; for You would not have formed anything You hated. 26 And how could anything endure if You had not willed it? Or how would what was not called by You be preserved? 27 You spare all things, for they are Yours, O Lord who love souls.
For Your great power is always at Your disposal; who can resist the strength of Your arm? [21]

There is no point of comparison between the great power of God and the power of man, for the power of God has its source not outside Himself, but He bears in Himself His strength and power, therefore it is at His disposal, He uses it as He wills. But the power of man is not from himself, but is a gift presented to him that will surely depart from him one day. For if he is struck with sickness or poverty or loses his social position, his strength departs with it or grows weak, and he becomes feeble. Many have had their arms and their spirits shattered, but as for God the Almighty, there is no one who can resist His arm!

Often man wrongs God because of his inability to know God's plan and thoughts, so he ascribes to Him weakness because of His long-suffering, or inability because of the tribulations and persecutions that He allows to come upon His Church or His children. He is the Almighty, able to do everything with surpassing power, but how unsearchable are His judgments, and His ways past finding out? (Rom 11:33); "for who hath known the mind of the Lord? or who hath been his counsellor?" (Rom 11:34).

It is said in the supplication of Mordecai to God: "You are Lord of all, and there is none who can resist Your might" (Add Esth 13:11). Judith says: "Who are you that you should tempt the Lord?" (Jdt 8:11). And the Apostle Paul says: "Nay but, O man, who art thou that repliest against God? Shall the thing formed say to him that formed it, Why hast thou made me thus?" (Rom 9:20).
For the whole world before You is as what tips the balance of the scales, and as a drop of the dew of the dawn that falls upon the earth. [22]

"Behold, the nations are as a drop of a bucket, and are counted as the small dust of the balance" (Isa 40:15). He likens God to one who holds a balance to put the whole world in one pan, and behold, it is like a drop of morning dew or the dust of the balance. And on the other hand He puts the whole world in one pan and man in the other pan, and there is no point of comparison or balance between them. God presents His love to man with great exactness, according to what is for his edification.
* On this hope our souls cleave to Him who is faithful in His promises, just in His judgments.
He who commanded us not to lie will not lie, for there is nothing that is impossible to Him except lying.
Let our faith be kindled within us that we may realize that everything is near to Him.
For by the word of His power He established all, and by His word He is able to destroy everything.
"Who shall say to Him, What have You done? Who can resist the strength of His authority?" (Wis 12:12; 11:22). He does what He wills and as He wills, and nothing opposes His command.

entries.section: 6. Beyond God's forbearance

paragraphs.text: St. Clement of Rome But You have mercy on all, because You are able to do all things, and You overlook the sins of men that they may repent. [23]

The mercy of God embraces all creation, for it is His work, so how much more does He show kindness to man, for whose sake He created all things. God is a lover of mankind even in His chastenings of them, for their goal is repentance (metanoia), which He seeks from all sinners, and not from a particular nation, for His door is open to all.

His view of mankind is wonderful, for men are the good creation of God, but their choice of evil isolates them from God, the source of their goodness. Therefore God continues to call them to repentance, that is, to return to Him, for they are the object of His love and mercy.

"You overlook" here means "You are long-suffering," for He does not will that men should perish, but that all should come to repentance (2 Pet 3:9). And when we return to Him in repentance, He says that He no longer remembers our sins.

entries.section: 6. Beyond God's forbearance

paragraphs.text: For You love all things that exist, and loathe nothing that You made; for You would not have formed anything You hated. [24]

God is Almighty, and cannot be resisted, and He is love itself toward all heavenly and earthly beings. By this view He prepares man to receive free salvation from God who loves the whole world by giving the only-begotten Son (Jn 3:16).

* The heavenly Father knows what we need before we ask Him (Mt 6:8). It is reasonable that He who is the Father of the world and its Creator, who loves all beings and loathes nothing that He made (Wis 11:24), provides what is for the benefit of each one without prayer to Him; He does this as a father who protects his little ones and does not wait for them to ask Him, whether they are altogether unable to ask Him, or because of their ignorance, for they often ask for what is entirely against their benefit.

Origen St. Augustine asks: If God hates nothing that He made, how was it said that He hated Esau? He answers this, saying: [God is the maker of all creatures. Every creature of God is good. Every man is a creature as man, not as a sinner. God is the Creator of both the body of man and his soul. Neither of them is evil, and God does not hate them. He hates nothing in man but sin. Sin in man is a distortion and disorder, that is, a straying from the Creator, who is the highest (from the soul), and a resort to the creatures lower than He (the lusts of the flesh and the love of the world, etc.). God hates Esau not as man, but as sinner.]

* The love with which God loves is beyond comprehension and unchanging. For He did not begin to love us from the time when we were reconciled to Him by the blood of His Son, but He loved us even before the foundation of the world, that we might become sons to Him with His only-begotten Son; He loved us even before there was any existence of ours. Let us not look at the reality of our reconciliation with God through the death of His Son, nor understand it as though the reconciliation of the Son to us with Him were accomplished in this manner: that He has now begun to love those whom He formerly hated, as though an enemy were reconciled with an enemy, and they became friends, and mutual love took the place of mutual hatred. Rather we were reconciled with Him who was already loving us, but we ourselves had become enemies because of our sins.

That you may realize that I speak the truth in this, let the Apostle bear witness, who says: "God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us" (Rom 5:8). So God bears love for us even when we were practicing enmity against Him, and doing iniquity.

It was said to Him with perfect truth: "Thou hatest all workers of iniquity" (Ps 5:5). So in a wonderful divine way, when we hated Him, He loved us. For He hated us in what we were, which He had not created us to be... He hates what we have made of ourselves, and loves what He has made in us!
This can be understood truly in the case of all, concerning Him to whom it was said with truth: "You hate nothing that You made" (Wis 11:24).

entries.section: 6. Beyond God's forbearance

paragraphs.text: St. Augustine And how could anything endure that You had not willed, or how be preserved if not called by You? [25]

Here the wonder of the love of God is brought out, for He created man that he might remain with Him, keeping him from every danger. For God wants man and loves him and protects him from every harm, and prepares a place for him in heaven.

* If there is a rich woman who possesses much wealth and a splendid house, yet finds no one to protect her, for many attack her wishing to inflict harm and ruin upon her. And because she cannot bear this harm and attack, she therefore seeks a strong husband who would be equal to this purpose, and trained in all respects. And when she finds such a man after much seeking, she rejoices in him greatly, and finds in him a fortress that protects her.
St. Macarius the Great

entries.section: 6. Beyond God's forbearance

paragraphs.text: You spare all things, for they are Yours, O Lord, lover of the living. [26]
The purpose of His creating man and the goal of it is man's being with God, as the son who rests in the bosom of his father full of tenderness toward him.
God is life; He possesses man for Himself and grants him life.

* God rules all creation (the earthly), but He did not establish His throne in it, nor did He enter into fellowship with it, but He was pleased with man alone, and entered into fellowship with him, and in him alone He rested... The wise soul, after passing through all creatures, finds no rest for itself except in the Lord alone, and the Lord also is not pleased with anyone but man alone.
St. Macarius the Great
Grant me Your wisdom, that I may perceive the mysteries of Your love!
* Your wisdom raised up a leader for Your people.
You gave them a holy prophet who works by Your Spirit!
Moses in his youth thought that he was able to save Your people!
In weakness he could not reconcile two brothers of Your enslaved people!
But Your wisdom supported him when he was an old man of eighty.
Wisdom moved him and renewed his inner youth.
He defied the violence of Pharaoh and the harshness of the wilderness.
The old man overcame kings, and enjoyed wonderful blessings!
Your wisdom, O my God, is able to raise up a hero from the weak!
Your wisdom shepherds Your people, and cares for every believer!
Your wisdom is the Good Shepherd, who raises up leaders from among the believers.
* Your people collapsed from thirst in the midst of the wilderness.
So waters burst forth for them from a flinty rock.
And they saw in it Your wisdom, which makes burst forth in its belly - the hard stones - springs of living waters of love.
