The unbelievers were deprived of wisdom, so the Nile offered them corrupt water mixed with the blood of the infants that they had shed!
And the believers enjoyed wisdom, so springs of living water burst forth in them!
The water of the Nile turned for the unbelievers into blood, and the water of the rock refreshed the believers and prepared them for life in the wilderness.
The unbelievers thirsted and died, and the believers thirsted and experienced life by You and with You!
* Without partiality You chasten; grant me to accept Your chastening from Your life-giving hands, that I may taste Your fatherhood, and respond to Your love for me.
That I may see You a Father who chastens in order to give life, and not a judge who punishes because You cannot bear sin.
* The wicked are troubled and grieve, for they count in their chastening a harshness that comes from You.
And Your righteous ones see You and rejoice in the midst of affliction, and experience Your love.
* You are wonderful, O wisdom of God, in Your tenderness, even with the wicked You are gentle and compassionate, You chasten and punish, but little by little.
For You created man, not to destroy him but to give him life.
You wait even for the wicked to return to You.
In firmness You chasten, that perhaps they may return to themselves, seek You and live.
* The ancient Egyptians worshiped animals and reptiles and insects.
From the kinds of their gods You punished them by their very sins, that sin might become bitter in their mouths.
You could have sent upon them beasts to devour them.
Or destroyed them with a word from Your mouth.
But You do not will the death of the sinner, but that he should return and live.
You sent them insects to trouble them, not to kill them.
For even while You chasten, You spare!
For Your creation is very dear to You.
Glory to You, O Lover of all mankind!

entries.section: 1. Between deification and admiration of the Creator

paragraphs.text: 23 Therefore the hypocrites who lived in foolishness, You tormented with their own abominations. 24 For they went astray farther than the ways of error, having taken as gods those creatures that their enemies despise, deceived like children who have no understanding. 25 Therefore You sent upon them, as upon children without reason, a judgment to mock them. 26 But they that would not be admonished by the correction of mockery shall feel a judgment worthy of God. 27 For when they suffered in their indignation, and saw that those whom they had taken to be gods were the means of their torment, they acknowledged the true God, whom they had formerly denied to know; and therefore the end of condemnation came upon them.
Surely all men who are ignorant of God are naturally vain, for they were not able to know Him who is from the good things that are seen, nor did they recognize the Maker by considering His works. [1]

Man did not know the explanation of natural phenomena: the power of the sun to give light, to warm and to purify, and to determine day and night; the power of fire to consume; the lightning that appears for moments and disappears, so that he supposed that the god was angry with men, and so on. All this led some to set up these powers and phenomena as gods. God warned His people against following the pagans in this matter: “Lest you lift up your eyes to heaven, and when you see the sun, and the moon, and the stars, even all the host of heaven, should be driven to worship them, and serve them, which the Lord your God has divided unto all nations under the whole heaven” (Deut 4:19).

Because man fell into this worship, the hymn of the Three Young Men in the fiery furnace came to deal with this matter, in which man offers praise to God, calling all creation to worship God with him.

“O all you works of the Lord, bless the Lord; praise Him and exalt Him above all for ever... O you heavens, bless the Lord... angels... sun and moon and stars... showers and dew... clouds and winds... fire and heat, etc.”
If man is amazed at the beauty and power of creation, it is fitting for him to praise its Creator, who showed such wonder in creating it for the sake of man.

Foolish are all men who fail to know God through their study of His works, considering His works themselves to be gods. Truly His works are great and glorious, but there is no ground for comparison between them and their Maker. The author did not offer rational or philosophical proofs of the existence of God, for it is a reality that is not a matter of discussion and debate, but a matter of experience and life.
In ignorance man put the beauty and power of the creatures in the place of the creativity of the Creator and His infinite power.

God speaks with mankind through His creation. As St. Paul says: “For the invisible things of Him from the creation of the world are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made, even His eternal power and Godhead; so that they are without excuse” (Rom 1:20). And David the prophet says: “The heavens declare the glory of God; and the firmament shows His handywork” (Ps 19:1). Pope Athanasius the Apostolic wrote: [By His Word (the Logos) God gave the world to be, so that men might be able to know Him through His works, He who by nature is invisible; for the artist, though he is not seen, is known by his works.]
* Creation itself, by its harmony and order, proclaims the greatness of the divine nature.

Father John of Damascus * How did God reveal Himself? By a voice from heaven? Not at all! God made a throne of splendor able to draw men more than a voice. He set before them the enormous creation, so that the wise and the unlearned, the Scythians and the barbarians, might ascend to God, learning through the sight of the beauty of the things they see.

St. John Chrysostom * It is fitting for all who live on this earth to begin by using the senses upon sensible things, that they may pass from them to the knowledge of intelligible things. But their knowledge must not stop at sensible things.

Origen * In all visible things clear reminders of the Maker of good things take hold of us. So we give no opportunity to sins, and leave no place in our hearts for the enemy, if we have God dwelling in us through our constant remembrance of Him.

St. Basil the Great * It is very easy to understand that the Creator of the angels, principalities and powers is He who in a moment of His power made all this great beauty of the world out of nothing, when it had no existence, and gave being to things and causes that did not exist.

St. Ambrose * The prophet also said: “The heavens declare the glory of God” (Ps 19:1). Will the pagans say at the judgment that they were ignorant of the existence of God? Did they not hear the heavens sending forth a voice through the harmony of the order of all things, speaking plainly as with a trumpet? Did you not see the hours of the night and the day remaining unchanged, and the good order of winter and spring and the other seasons standing firm and unmoved...? Yet God did not make this great order so in order to teach the pagans so that they might be without excuse, but He set it forth that they might come to know Him. But by failing to recognize Him they deprive themselves of any excuse.

entries.section: 1. Between deification and admiration of the Creator

paragraphs.text: St. John Chrysostom But they deemed either fire, or wind, or the swift air, or the circle of the stars, or the violent water, or the lights of heaven, to be the gods which govern the world. [2]

What concerns the author is not only that God is Creator, but that being the Creator He cares for His creation. Life does not proceed by chance nor by an inevitable fate, as many of the philosophers and astrologers thought; some suppose that the spheres or other things govern the world by an unavoidable decree, but God in His fatherhood watches over the world and cares for it.

* The pagans tried to reach heaven, but since they shattered the light that was in them, and instead committed themselves to the darkness of their own minds, they sought the immaterial in bodies, and the unlimited in created forms, and by this they lost their harmony with the light.

St. John Chrysostom * Moses began to speak, saying: In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth (Gen 1:1). After that the teacher began to record what happened in the six days of the creative power. By prophecy of lofty vision he beheld the Hidden One calling what was nothing to rise and become something; and the signs and the voices that were directed to the creatures, Moses heard and saw by the light of prophecy. He had entered into the treasury of divinity like a steward, and the riches of the creative power were not hidden from him; and as he saw and as he heard in the exalted place, so the teacher who preaches concerning the creatures set it down in his book.

He said: In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth, and proved that the world has an origin and a beginning. From Mount Sinai Moses brought down to the world, which had been darkened by idolatry, a teaching full of light. When creatures of every shape were being worshipped, they were counted like gods in their natures; the world was darkened by the love of vain idols, creation forgot its Maker and He was no longer remembered, and men worshipped either fire, or water, or the stars, or animals, or birds.

entries.section: 1. Between deification and admiration of the Creator

paragraphs.text: St. Mar Jacob of Serugh If they supposed those to be gods because they were delighted with their beauty, let them know how much greater their Lord is than they, for He who created them is the source of beauty. [3]

Men were charmed by the beauty of creation and did not contemplate the love of the Creator. Therefore the Word of God, the Creator, came down to them, that by His practical love on the Cross He might draw them out of error and bring them into the divine truth.

* A cloud of errors covered their hearts. For while they ought to have honored the Creator of all through the beautiful creatures that He brought into being, they clung to what they had, saying that the things they were able to see were sufficient for their salvation.

Ambrosiaster * Your rays went forth to all quarters and gave them light, and behold, the peoples delight in Your light which has gladdened them; Your rays scattered all the darkness of idol worship and set up for You the image of light among those in darkness. You sent a message to the Magi by a star of light, and drew them and brought them out of darkness into Your light. Your messenger ran to preach to those in darkness, and prepared there the way for Your shining, that You might walk in it (Zech 6:12)...

He sent the light to kill the darkness in its place, and to make a path in the wilderness of idol worship. He cast a single ray of His lights upon the land, and by His shining scattered the strong night of error. He came to enlighten all the world by His birth, and first sent to the beginning of the earth (the Far East) that they might come to Him. He sent a messenger of light and preachers to the land far from teaching, to bring it so that it might be guided; He laid on the shoulder of the barbarians the yoke of the report, and set them on the road that they might come to His service...
The idols of Egypt saw the Savior and trembled and feared Him, as had been preached beforehand by prophecy (Isa 19:1)...

The pillars of Egypt that bore the idols all trembled before Him who came to break them by His crucifixion; all the platforms of sacrifices were destroyed by the high priest who came to the slaughter that He might abolish them. The Truth entered and whispered (in the ears of) the idols and terrified them, and called them to fall though they do not hear. Such things were said on the part of Justice to the idols of Egypt, rich in prostrations:

Fall down, you weak one; it is enough that you have conquered by metaphors. He to whom worship is due has come; leave Him the place that He may stand upon His kingdom. You dried husks, empty the place for the Son of God. You who were fashioned by error, come down from your palaces. You corrupt idols that have become snares for those who worship you, be broken and do not hunt any more for corruption. You weak one, flee from the Mighty One who has come to you, and stand no more in the place of the King who has arrived. You manufactured thing, you that took the name of God and troubled the earth, behold the Maker has come down from His place to put you to shame. The wind has gone out to gather the thorns from the fields; flee, you tares, from the tempest, the lady of the quarters. The host of idol worship feared the Mighty One, and the ranks of the idols were told the good news of their fall.

entries.section: 1. Between deification and admiration of the Creator

paragraphs.text: St. Mar Jacob of Serugh And if they were amazed at their power and working, let them understand from them how much more powerful is He who formed them. [4]

Man, fallen from his position, his dignity and his glory, loses the things that God gave him, and stands looking at nature and what is in it as though it were spirit; this has been called animism. So he worshipped stones, rivers and springs, as he worshipped trees and animals. In short, whenever he admired a power or a beauty or a particular trait in some being, he worshipped it. We mention by way of example:
The calf as a symbol of procreation.
The serpent as a symbol of the renewal of life, since it sheds its outer skin and a new skin takes its place, giving it vitality and energy.
The eagle and the falcon as a symbol of wisdom and of seeing from afar.
Natural phenomena such as storms, winds and fire as a symbol of the power that man cannot resist.
Sex and prostitution for the satisfaction of bodily lusts in unrestrained licentiousness.
Emperors, kings and heroes, even after their death.
Man often stands before nature amazed at its power and working, but it is fitting for him to realize the power of its wonderful Creator.

entries.section: 1. Between deification and admiration of the Creator

paragraphs.text: For by the greatness and beauty of the creatures proportionally the Maker of them is seen. [5]
The greatness and beauty that characterize creation reveal the greatness of its Creator!

* “For the invisible things of Him from the creation of the world are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made, even His eternal power and Godhead” (Rom 1:20). What he means is this: He set His creation in the midst, before the eyes of men, that they might perceive the Creator from His works. Another writer pointed to the same: “For by the greatness and beauty of the creatures proportionally (relatively) the Maker of them is seen” (Wis 13:5). Behold the greatness. Marvel at the power of its Maker! Do you see the beauty? Be amazed at the wisdom of its Creator! This is what the prophet meant when he said: “The heavens declare the glory of God” (Ps 19:1).

St. John Chrysostom * He Himself, being above all, the Ruler and King and Governor of power, does everything for the glory of His Father and for the knowledge of Him, so that even through the works themselves He teaches us.

* We learn from the creatures without asking voices from them, but as we hear the Holy Scriptures we believe, and by seeing the order of all things and their harmony we know that this is the Creator, Lord and God of all beings, and we perceive His astonishing providence and His sovereignty over all.

Pope Athanasius the Apostolic * It is impossible for human eyes to see the divine nature, but they perceive its power to some extent through His divine works. Solomon says: “For by the greatness and beauty of the creatures proportionally the Maker of them is seen.”

He did not say that the Creator is seen through His creation, but made clear that this is “proportionally,” for God is too great to be comprehended by any man through his beholding the greatness of creation. And as his heart is lifted up the more by beholding more (of the greatness of creation), he receives a greater knowledge of God.
* Refute those who blaspheme the wise and good Creator, and recognize from what you hear and read and discover that “from the greatness and beauty of creation its Maker is known proportionally.”

And as we bow our knees with good reverence before the Maker of the worlds, I mean the world of sense and the world of thought, what is seen and what is not seen, you glorify God with a holy tongue that murmurs of what is known, and lips that do not keep silent, and a heart that does not tire, saying: “How great are Your works, O Lord. In wisdom You have made them all”; honor and glory and majesty are due to You from now through all ages. Amen.

entries.section: 1. Between deification and admiration of the Creator

paragraphs.text: St. Cyril of Jerusalem Yet these men are less to be blamed, for they perhaps err only because they seek God and desire to find Him. [6]

Here the wise man has compassion on the pagans who were drawn to the greatness of creation, its power and its beauty, and at the beginning gave them a kind of excuse. Perhaps their aim was God Himself, and when they sought Him in creation they were dazzled by its beauty and turned aside from their goal.

The wise man went back to rebuke them, for though he gave them something of an excuse, he looks to what God gave them, namely the mind, which is able to pass beyond the limits of visible things to believe in Him who is invisible, if they had been sincere in seeking the truth.

entries.section: 1. Between deification and admiration of the Creator

paragraphs.text: For they search diligently among His works, and are persuaded by the sight, because the things that are seen are beautiful. [7]
Solomon, characterized by tenderness and compassion, again offered the pagans an excuse because of the attractive allurement of the beauty of creation.

entries.section: 1. Between deification and admiration of the Creator

paragraphs.text: Yet even they are not to be pardoned. [8]

As the wise man looks at the pagans who desire to find God and search for Him diligently, he excuses them to some extent; but when he finds them behaving without reason because of their attraction to temporal beauty and pleasures, he declares their condemnation and that there is no pardon for them as long as they do not return to Him.

entries.section: 1. Between deification and admiration of the Creator

paragraphs.text: For if they were able to know so much, that they could discern the essence of the world, how did they not more quickly find the Lord of it? [9]

What increases their responsibility in not knowing God is that they investigate the sciences of nature and perceive some of its secrets, whereas it was fitting for them to seek God, for knowing Him is quicker and easier than knowing the secrets of the universe.
God created man as lord of the earthly creation, and gave him a mind that he might come to know the secrets of the universe and enjoy knowledge.
Solomon the wise commends research in the sciences and the knowledge of the laws of nature, for God did not create the mind that we might bury it, but as a gift that we kindle for edification.

The matter does not stop at knowing the secrets of the universe, but the believer passes beyond nature, to enjoy the knowledge of heavenly things and taste the sweetness of their pledge, and experience fellowship with the Heavenly One, the Creator of heaven and earth.

The wise man grieves at the degradation to which man has come: instead of rising to heavenly things he sank down into pagan worship, which denies the true God and drives man to wallow in abominations, even to violence and the shedding of blood.
* In the hearts of the Gentiles the honor of the one purest God was changed into a bloody worship of various gods.

Father Caesarius, Bishop of Arles * The world is beautiful without doubt, and lofty in the majesty of its size as in the order of its components, whether those in the oblique circle or those in the north or in its spherical shape. But it is not this but its Maker whom we must worship. If your subjects come to you, they cannot neglect to offer submission to you, who are their rulers and lords, and those who obtain from you what they wish present themselves to the greatness of your court. And if they have the opportunity to come to the royal house, they cast an admiring glance at its beautiful building, but they offer respect to you as “all in all.”

You, O kings, build your palaces and adorn them for yourselves, but the world was not created because God needs it. For God is everything in Himself: light unapproachable, a perfect world, power and mind.

If the world is a musical instrument moving in a well measured time, then I worship the Being who gave it this harmony, and played upon it the musical note, and sang its harmonious phrases, and I do not worship the instrument itself.
In musical contests the judges do not crown the lyres, ignoring the players upon them...

If anyone perceives the various elements of the world as powers of God, we do not approach the powers to offer them submission, but offer it to their Maker and Lord. I do not ask of matter what it cannot give, nor do I pass over God and give honor to the elements, which are unable to do anything other than what was appointed for them.
For despite the beauty of their appearance because of the skill of their Creator, they still bear the nature of matter...
While I admire the heavens and their elements for their creative design, I do not worship them as gods, knowing that the law of perishing rules over them.
Athenagoras

entries.section: 2. The deification of dead human work

paragraphs.text: 10 But miserable are they, and their hope is in dead things, who called them gods, which are the works of men's hands, gold and silver, the inventions of art, and the likenesses of beasts, or a useless stone, the work of an ancient hand. 11 Now a carpenter cuts down a tree from the forest, fit for the work, and skillfully strips off all its bark, and then with good craft makes it into a vessel serviceable for the uses of life, 12 and uses the leavings of his work to dress his food. 13 Then he takes a piece of what is left, which is good for nothing, a crooked piece of wood and full of knots, and carves it with diligence in his idle hours, and shapes it by the skill of his craft into the form of a man, 14 or makes it like some vile beast, smearing it with vermilion, and with paint coloring it red, and covering every stain in it. 15 And he makes for it a fitting place, and sets it in the wall, and fastens it with iron, 16 taking heed that it not fall, knowing that it cannot help itself, for it is an image and has need of help. 17 Then he prays to it concerning his goods and his wives and his children, and is not ashamed to speak to that which has no soul. 18 For health he asks of that which is weak, and for life he entreats that which is dead, and for help he implores that which is utterly unable to help, 19 and for a journey he begs of that which cannot walk, and for gain and trade and success in his undertakings he asks ability of that which is of all things the least able.

After speaking of the deification of creation or of some creatures or natural phenomena, he now speaks of the deification of human work, such as idols and statues. In speaking of creation he perhaps found an excuse to offer for them, though this excuse is unacceptable, because they ought to have been occupied with the Creator and not the creation, however great its beauty or power, and it was fitting for them to use their minds that God gave them, and so perceive what is beyond creation. But for man to worship a statue of wood or metal or stone is absurdity and misery.

But how miserable are those who set their hope on dead things, and called the works of men's hands gods, gold and silver skillfully made, and images of beasts, or a useless stone, the work of an ancient hand. [10]

The folly of man has reached the point that he enslaves himself to what he makes with his own hands, dead things. Goldsmiths and silversmiths, or sculptors, or carpenters, labor skillfully to fashion a dead idol. It is written in the book of Jeremiah the prophet: “For the customs of the people are vain: for one cuts a tree out of the forest, the work of the hands of the workman, with the axe. They deck it with silver and with gold; they fasten it with nails and with hammers, that it move not. They are upright as the palm tree, but speak not: they must needs be borne, because they cannot go. Be not afraid of them; for they cannot do evil, neither also is it in them to do good” (Jer 10:3-5).

* God put the knowledge of Himself in human hearts from the beginning. But this knowledge they foolishly poured into wood and stones, and by this they corrupted the truth, at least as far as they were able, while the truth is firm and unchanging, having its unchanging glory.

St. John Chrysostom * Like a wise physician, before speaking of the disease he pointed to its causes and its source. To prepare for the criticism of their evil, he began by pointing to the sources of their weakness: greed and deceit and corrupt assemblies, showing little by little the things that made them fall into the pit of destruction, when he adds: “the work of their own hands” (Isa 2:8). For what is more absurd than to see a man making a god? Holy Scripture is accustomed to call idols “abominations” (Mt 24:15; Dan 11:31; 12:11).
St. John Chrysostom In (Isaiah 44) he spoke of the need of a smith and a carpenter and other skilled workmen to make the idol that the pagans worship.

entries.section: 2. The deification of dead human work

paragraphs.text: Now a skillful woodcutter saws down a tree easy to handle, and skillfully strips off all its bark, and then with good craft makes it into a vessel serviceable for the uses of life. [11]
The skill of carpenters is a gift from God, but in their full freedom they can misuse this gift...

It was fitting for the carpenter to use his skill in making household or farming tools, or for sailing, such as ships, and so on, for the benefit of mankind; but to make of them a statue to take the place of the Creator is a crime and a transgression of the divine commandment.

* By worshipping things of wood and stone they do not see that, while they trample under foot and burn what in no way differs from them, they call parts of these materials gods. And what they were using in their service a short time before, they carve and worship in their folly, without seeing or thinking at all that they are not worshipping gods but the work of a turner.

For as long as the stone is not hewn and the wood is not worked, they tread upon the one and use the other for their various purposes, even in base uses. But when the craftsman fashions them according to his skill, and shapes the material into the form of a man or a woman, then, thanking the craftsman, they begin to worship them as gods, after they had bought them from the turner for a price. And besides this, the maker of images often prays to his own creations, as though he had forgotten the work that he himself finished, and calls gods those which he was cutting and carving and turning a short time before.

entries.section: 2. The deification of dead human work

paragraphs.text: Pope Athanasius the Apostolic And uses the leavings of it to dress his food, and is filled. [12]
He does not deny the role of the carpenter in making useful wooden tools; even the leavings are used as fuel for cooking food.

In Isaiah 44 the prophet portrays for us how they use the wood, part of it for warmth, another for cooking food, and the rest they make into a god, an idol, before which they fall down and worship, and pray to it, saying: “Deliver me; for You are my god” (Isa 44:17).

* If it were a god, all the trees would have to be divine. Why then do you use what is left of the wood to obtain a fire that serves you in preparing food...? Do you not put wood in the fire, of the same kind of wood to which you pay worship? How then do you cast away the one and worship the other? Rightly he adds: “They have not known nor understood: for He has shut their eyes, that they cannot see; and their hearts, that they cannot understand. And none considers in his heart, neither is there knowledge nor understanding to say, I have burned part of it in the fire...” (Isa 44:18-19).

entries.section: 2. The deification of dead human work

paragraphs.text: Father Theodoret, Bishop of Cyrrhus But a castaway piece that is good for nothing, a crooked piece of wood and full of knots, he takes and carves with diligence in his idle hours, and shapes it with skill that he may gain times of rest, and makes it the form of a man. [13]

In some detail he describes how the idol is made; in irony he shows that it is not made even of a precious stone, but of the refuse of trees. As for his saying: “skill that he may gain times of rest,” it means that man, having become inwardly empty, finds nothing useful to practice, and so exercises his craft in fashioning a statue. Truly the inner emptiness is behind atheism!

The wise man portrays a carpenter who goes to the forest and chooses a tree or some of its branches, cuts it down, and takes it to his house or his workshop. He divides it into parts and slabs and then strips off the outer covering of the tree, and after using it to make some utensil for the house or for farming, and so on, he looks for a castaway piece, not to use it as fuel, but to make of it a statue that he worships.

Here he alludes to the vanity of emperors and kings, who make statues of themselves that men may worship them in their lifetime and after their death; by this they think that they exercise lordship over the people even after their death. At the same time some simple people in their weakness think that their lives are in the hands of these mighty ones even after their death.
In contempt of idolaters the author shows that an idol can be made from the refuse of wood, and in this there is shame!

* He says (Isa 44:13) that he copies (for the idol) not divine but human features, and forms a human image and worships his own image as a god. Then the prophet Isaiah teaches us (Isa 44:14) that the forests that are on the mountains were given by the Creator to men, that they might be permitted to use them to kindle fire and serve the needs of their bodies. But these, on the contrary, take evergreen branches, or an oak, or a pine tree, which the God of the universe planted and supplied with rain for the benefit of man and to provide him with many material goods, yet they use them to make gods.

entries.section: 2. The deification of dead human work

paragraphs.text: Father Theodoret, Bishop of Cyrrhus Or makes it like some vile beast, smearing it with crimson, and with paint coloring its surface red, and covering every blemish in it. [14]

What adds to the absurdity of the matter is that the carpenter makes a statue not of an emperor or a king but of an animal or some trivial insect, and shows skill in carving and forming the statue, and man falls down before it and worships it, and offers it sacrifices and offerings.

They saw in birds and animals certain symbols. The falcon and the eagle are known for sharpness of sight, so they symbolized wisdom and far-sightedness. The calf symbolizes fertility, and the serpent life, since it changes its skin from time to time.

entries.section: 2. The deification of dead human work

paragraphs.text: And makes for it a shrine fitting for it, and sets it in the wall, and fastens it with iron. [15]

In a new contempt he mocks those who busy themselves with making shrines fastened with nails on the wall in order that the statues may be kept in them lest they fall and be broken. For the statue is unable to bear itself, so the nails bear it.
The author mocks the place or dwelling that is fastened with iron on a wall for the idol to be put in it.
By his saying: “fitting for it” he mocks the statue, for which nothing is fitting except to be set as upon a wall, having no work and no power to move.

entries.section: 2. The deification of dead human work

paragraphs.text: Taking care lest it fall, knowing that it cannot help itself, for it is an image and has need of help! [16]
A statue that needs iron nails to fasten it or its shrine in the wall, and whose owner fears its falling, how can it raise up those who fall?

The wise man exposes the weakness of the pagan gods: they are unable to help themselves, so how can they help those who worship them? These dead gods, how can they give life to others, and being unable to move, how can they support man in his movements and his journeys?
Holy Scripture in both its Testaments, as well as church history through the ages down to our present day, has shown us how God desires to restore man to his first dominion in the Garden of Eden.
We give a few examples here:

God gave Joshua the son of Nun authority to stop the motion of some of the heavenly bodies, that the day might be lengthened and he might gain victory over the wicked who resisted the divine truth (Josh 10).

God gave Elijah the prophet authority, so that he brought down fire that consumed the captains of fifty and their men, because they were arrogant against God Himself in the person of His prophet (2 Kgs 1:10), and also he asked for fire from heaven to consume a sacrifice, to bring the people back to the true knowledge of God (1 Kgs 18:38). As He gave him.
God gave many of the saints authority over nature and wild animals, but within limits lest they fall into pride. Among these was St. Anasimon, with whom lions made friends.
* O what dangerous folly! What kind of gods are these gods of yours, which can be stolen? Are you not ashamed to say: “Why did you steal them?”

entries.section: 2. The deification of dead human work

paragraphs.text: St. John Chrysostom And when he wants to pray for his goods and his marriage and his children, he is not ashamed to address that which has no soul, and for health he implores that which is weak. [17]

God looks upon men for whose sake He created the world with all its possibilities and beauty, and sees them asking a piece of wood to support them in the management of their money or their married life or their children or for their healing, while this statue is lifeless, having no life in it, and unable even to move.

In amazement the author mocks him who asks health of an idol in which there is no life, and asks strength of what has no strength, and asks help of what has no experience, and asks protection on his journeys of an idol unable to move.

entries.section: 2. The deification of dead human work

paragraphs.text: And for life he entreats that which is dead, and for help he implores that which has no experience at all, and for a successful journey, that which cannot take a step. [18]

* What is more absurd than these men? Though they have been given a mind, and enjoy wonderful privileges from the compassions of God, they worship a lifeless stone, and are far from being ashamed or feeling any absurdity. They deal with it as with dumb beasts. Therefore Paul also wrote these words: “You know that you were Gentiles, carried away to these dumb idols, even as you were led” (1 Cor 12:2). Rightly he said: “dumb”; people who have the gift of speech, who enjoy reason and hearing, resort to things that have not these qualities, but resemble dumb animals. What excuse can such men have?

entries.section: 2. The deification of dead human work

paragraphs.text: St. John Chrysostom And for gain and enterprise and the success of his hands' work, he seeks strength of that which has no strength in its hands. [19]

The man who has died through sin needs One who is able to raise him from death; he who is exposed to troubles from satanic wars and sicknesses and afflictions needs One who lifts him above pain and brings him across to the blessed life; he who walks through life as on a passing journey needs One able to lift him to heaven; and he who needs strength for work and ability to think in order to succeed needs that Almighty One who gives strength. Who is able to give all this to man except the incarnate Word of God and His heavenly wisdom! How can man exchange this heavenly One who loves mankind for a dead statue unable to lead itself?!

* “For they have sown the wind, and they shall reap the whirlwind: it has no stalk; the bud shall yield no meal” (Hos 8:7)... there is no fruit to gather as your harvest from the service of the idol; as for their sheaves, they are like ears of wheat shattered by the wind: many stalks appear outwardly, but there is not a single seed in them. Such is the nature of idolatry: on one side it can take the form of a man or a woman, or a lion or any other animal through art (sculpture), and on the other side it is deprived of any power or energy.
Theodoret, Bishop of Cyrrhus

entries.section: Idol worship in Isaiah 44

paragraphs.text: Isaiah chapter 44 gives us a wonderful picture of the corruption of idol worship, showing that the idols and their makers and those who worship them all bear shame and vanity. The makers of idols are earnest, regarding neither hunger nor thirst nor weariness (Isa 44:12), as they make the axe from iron and beat out plates to set up statues. So also with the carpenters, who spend every effort to carve wooden statues. All of them toil and do not tire to set up metal or wooden statues unable to give salvation, while the children of God are lax in their spiritual striving, though they enjoy divine possibilities able to bring them to the enjoyment of eternal salvation. It is as though these laborers in vain condemn the lax children of God, as the Lord of glory Jesus said that the children of this generation are wiser than the children of the Kingdom (Lk 16:8).

On another side, making metal statues exhausts the energy of the workmen, while making wooden statues is accompanied by amusement with what is left over of the wood, since it is used in the hearth for warmth or for cooking food, at the very time in which they quiet their conscience by worshipping the wood carved into a statue.
Finally, what does the worship of idols (or withdrawal from God) offer:
a- Blindness of inner insight and inner darkness (Isa 44:18), while Christ is the Sun of Righteousness (Mal 4:2).
b- Ignorance and lack of knowledge (Isa 44:19), while Christ is our righteousness.
c- Hunger, so that man eats ashes (Isa 44:20), while the Lord Christ is the heavenly bread.
d- Lying and deceit and misleading (Isa 44:20), while the Lord Christ is the Way and the Truth.

In other words, we find in our Christ inner enlightenment, knowledge, satisfaction, truth and all our needs, but outside Him there is nothing but inner emptiness, a feeling of isolation and loss of inner insight.

* He shows (Isa 44:12-13) that the forming of what are called gods depends on many resources. For their maker needs a smith to prepare the tools and a grinder to make the tools sharp. And on his part, as a skilled craftsman, he needs coal and fire to help him. Besides this, the maker of these things experiences the desire to eat and drink. All these successive things are necessary to make a god for fools to worship.
Father Theodoret, Bishop of Cyrrhus
You are the Supreme Good
* My soul thirsts for the good, and will keep praising You for the abundance of Your generosity.
All that is around me bears witness to Your love for me, and Your surpassing care.
You gave me this beautiful world; You offered me every possibility of a happy life.
You have not withheld from me anything of the works of Your honor.
The earth and the oceans and the firmament and space and all the planets cry out, speaking to me in the language of creation about You, O heavenly Artist!
The voice of nature does not leave my ear!
Glory to You, my wonderful Creator!
* In folly my fathers worshipped the creation and not its Creator.
They turned their backs to You, and deified what You gave them.
They worshipped the gift, not the Giver!
The beauty and power of the work of Your hands dazzled them; instead of praising You, they praised perishing beings!
Why should I lay the blame on my fathers, when I complain of myself to You.
Often I have enslaved myself to what You gave me; instead of ruling over temporal things, I became by my own will a slave to them.
It ruled me instead of my ruling it.
It moves me like a toy in its hands, instead of my moving it for the edification of my soul.
Restore to me my freedom and my dignity, and the wisdom that You gave me.
* How can I worship what has no life, and leave You, O eternal Life?
You are the Creator of all and the Giver of life.
Let me possess You, for You are the Supreme Good.
You are the Giver of authority and freedom.
You are the One who satisfies soul and body together!
You are my all.
* Enter the door of my heart, so that no other has a place in it.
Occupy it, and establish Your kingdom within it.
Declare Your glory and Your authority in me.
Enter and dwell in it, that I may abide in You.
Rest within me, that I may rest in Your divine bosom!
* My God, my soul has no bridegroom but You!
I have no strength except in You.
I have no incorruption except by union with You.
I have no gain except by possessing You!
Let me worship You with all my being: let my body glorify You, and my soul praise You, and my will, which You have sanctified, sing to You!
Finally I cry to You, hasten and come, O Beloved of my soul, for my heart shall not cling to the love of the world.
It awaits its swift passage to You.
Come to me, and I will come to You by Your Holy Spirit!

entries.section: 1. The ship or the wooden idol?

paragraphs.text: 1 And another, before he sails on the sea and goes upon the raging waves, calls upon a piece of wood more fragile than the vessel that carries him. 2 For the vessel was devised by the desire for gain, and the wisdom of the craftsman built it; 3 but Your providence, O Father, is that which governs it, for You have made a way in the sea, and a safe path in the waves, 4 showing that You can save from every danger, even if a man should go to sea without skill. 5 And You love that the works of Your wisdom should not be in vain; therefore men entrust their lives to a very small piece of wood, and pass over the deep in a ship and are saved. 6 For in the beginning also, when the proud giants perished, the hope of the world fled to a ship, and Your hand guided it, and left to all ages a seed of generations. 7 For blessed is the wood by which righteousness comes; 8 but the wood that is made an idol is cursed, both it and he that made it: he, because he made it; and it, because, being corruptible, it was called god. 9 For the ungodly and his ungodliness are alike hateful to God, 10 and the thing made shall be punished with him that made it. 11 Therefore there shall be a visitation also upon the idols of the Gentiles, because in the creation of God they have become an abomination, and a stumbling block to the souls of men, and a snare to the feet of the foolish. Here the wise man speaks of those who are skillful in building ships, and then fix a wooden image of the god at the prow or the stern of the ship, supposing that it is able to protect the ship, and offering it daily sacrifices.

The Book of Acts (Acts 28:11) refers to such a matter, where it mentions an Alexandrian ship marked with the sign of Gemini or the Twin Brothers, who were regarded as the sons of the Greek god Zeus, Castor and Pollux. The sailors used to set their image on their ships as two gods who preserve ships from sinking.

God gave man the skill to build ships with wisdom, as He gave this skill to those who made the tabernacle of meeting (Ex 31:3; 35:31, 35; Wis 8:6). But it is God who preserves the ship, for the wisdom of God is what leads the world on land and sea and in the air and space.
And another, before he sails on the sea and goes upon the raging waves, calls upon a piece of wood more fragile than the vessel that carries him. [1]

He gives the example of the sailor who calls upon a wooden god whose material is worse than the wood from which his ship was made. Thus the author mocks the idol itself, as well as the one who takes refuge in it.
What folly, that man should resort for help in the midst of the sea to the wood of an idol, instead of trusting in the wood of the ship, which is built and steered with wisdom from above...
How can the weak protect one who is stronger than he? These wooden gods are far weaker than the ship, and therefore weaker than the man who made the ship.

entries.section: 1. The ship or the wooden idol?

paragraphs.text: For the desire of gain devised this vessel, and the artisan wisdom built it. [2]

The wise man compares the maker of the ship with the maker of the wooden idol. Both the ship and the wooden idol are the work of man and reveal his skill. But the first offered what is for the benefit of mankind, since there is need of sailing, whether for fishing or for travel between the coastal countries, while the second spoils his time with what corrupts the minds of the simple.

It is fitting for the makers of idols not to waste their gifts and skill and abilities on defective idols that are of no use, but to use them for what edifies mankind, such as shipbuilding, and so on.

entries.section: 1. The ship or the wooden idol?

paragraphs.text: But Your providence, O Father, is what guides it, for You have made a way even in the sea, and in the waves a safe path. [3]

Here he calls the divine wisdom “divine providence,” for the wisdom of God is infinite love. For the first time the expression “divine providence” appears in the Bible, though it is an idea that the Bible affirms in both the Old and New Testaments (Josh 4:24; 1 Kgs 18:46).
Divine providence means the divine love ever working on behalf of the creation beloved by God, and it is a creative work.

God's surpassing providence appeared when He set up a way for His people and believers, and a safe path in the waves, which Noah and his family experienced in the midst of the Flood, and the people of Israel during their Exodus and their crossing of the Red Sea into the wilderness.
In the midst of the waves of the sea of this world the believer leans on the breast of God, the Creator of land and sea, and is at peace, sheltered under the wings of divine providence.

Jonah the prophet found no way sweeter and safer than that which God gave him when the sailors cast him into the raging sea. The Lord had prepared a great fish to swallow him (Jon 1:17). Inside it he enjoyed a unique ship not made by man; he lifted his heart to God and enjoyed what the high priests did not enjoy in the Holy of Holies, for he says: “My prayer came in unto You, into Your holy temple” (Jon 2:7). He offered a unique hymn of the joy of the resurrection: “Salvation is of the Lord” (Jon 2:9). St. Jacob of Serugh sees him as a deposit kept in the belly of the fish. Where there is no hope, hope in the Lord was revealed before him, and where death was found, it touched the new, risen life!

* Then the Lord prepared a fish, as it is written, and it swallowed Jonah to magnify him amid the waves. A great fish received him in amazement, and kept him as a deposit so that the waves surrounding him might not buffet him.
In the place where he had no hope, hope met him, and from within death life sprang forth by a hidden symbol.
In the place where there was no covering and no savior, tenderness covered him, that he might recover life from death.
* Jonah went on the fearful road without a companion. And mercies followed him and became his companions...
He hurried on his way to a terrifying place without fear. And where there are no saviors or keepers, the Lord kept the son of the Hebrews that he might not be corrupted...
A new ship Jonah acquired that was not broken, and he sat and went swiftly in the heart of the sea.
A marvelous ship that dives and probes the depths of the sea, and its cargo is kept, no harm reaching it.
A ship moving not by the winds on the face of the waters but by the heat within the waters without sailors.
He dwelt in a house that moves among the waves in amazement, and when it turns over it does not empty what is in it.
* His speech is marvelous, a priest praying at length, and his temple among the waves in haste.
The altar inside the fish, and the voice instead of offerings, and the Holy of Holies which none enters but one (the high priest).
A temple built by none but One who was born within the waters. The priest came from the dry land and entered and sanctified in it.

In the tabernacle there is Aaron, and on the top of the mountain Elijah, and in the temple Solomon, and inside the fish Jonah. It is a virgin altar in which no one has entered to serve as priest since the priest, radiant in his unique service, entered it.
A marvelous speech, when (Jonah) thundered in the belly of the fish, and his prayer went up, and there was nothing to hinder it.
His prayer cleft the depths, and the seas did not hinder it; it flew to the heights, and the great deep did not drown it.
It pressed on and entered among the angels and was not prevented. The ranks of the fiery ones met it and it was not rebuked.

(The prayer) bound its hands, and cried out in pain before the divine majesty. It bowed its head and asked mercy of the divine tenderness. It was troubled, and its voice thundered with supplication upon its sweet harp, and its mouth spoke asking for mercies. “My Lord, that servant imprisoned at the bottom of the sea sent me, and I have come to present the petition.”

entries.section: 1. The ship or the wooden idol?

paragraphs.text: St. Jacob of Serugh Showing that You can save from every danger, even if a man should go to sea without skill. [4]
Jonah had no skill to steer a fish in the sea, being in its belly, but he realized that the true Pilot is He who prepared the fish for him.

He saved him from danger, and even brought him into surpassing glories. And God saved His people of old, who lived in Egypt tending cattle and had no experience of the seas, so that they walked on dry ground in the midst of the waters, where no human feet had passed before and none passed after in this surpassing manner. How great is God's care and His love for us, even when we have no skill in crossing dangerous ways!

entries.section: 1. The ship or the wooden idol?

paragraphs.text: You love that the works of Your wisdom should not be barren, and therefore men entrust their lives to a small piece of wood, and cross the waves on a raft and are saved. [5]

It is out of God's love for us that He uses small things for our salvation, that we may feel His providence and not rely on our abilities, as though we were able to save ourselves by our own human efforts. Often large ships become a place of danger for those on them, and the travelers, like the sailors, resort to simple pieces of wood that cannot be compared with the greatness of the ship, and those who escape the danger feel that they were carried not on pieces of wood but on the divine arms. In the midst of the dangerous waves the Apostle Paul says: “we let her drive” (Acts 27:15).

entries.section: 1. The ship or the wooden idol?

paragraphs.text: And in the beginning, when the proud giants were perishing, the hope of the world took refuge on a raft, and Your hand guided it, and left to all ages a seed of generations. [6]

The wise man often refers to the story of the Flood, in which wicked men supposed in their pride that there was none who could restrain them from their evils, and they perished in the Flood. But Noah and his family, that is, the company of believers, entered the wooden ark as though it were a lifebuoy, and passed through the destructive period of the Flood, to go out into a world renewed for their service. God preserved these eight souls for the renewal of mankind.

* When the work of the builders went on and drew near its end, the wicked laughed at the venerable man and mocked him. He was telling them what he heard from God, and they multiplied insults to his teaching. My brethren, perhaps they thought him mad, since he multiplied his warnings, and they threw mockery at his ark. He sighed over the wicked because they were ignorant, and they laughed at the work that he was carrying out. He began to build the new chamber from planks set in order according to measures he took from God; the building rose and was finished after a hundred years, and then all the work was completed (Gen 5:32; 6:8, 11). The voice of Noah the righteous became hoarse as he preached, and the sons of iniquity neglected and sinned the more. He offered them teaching as far as he could, and the iniquity of the earth was multiplying more and more. His great work bore witness to his words, and no comic tale was being told by the righteous man; that marvelous perfection which he made showed the truth he spoke. It was necessary for the wicked generation to know that Noah was not laboring in vain in his work. Their eyes despised the great sight, and their ears despised the preaching; they did not understand by the work that was done there, nor were they guided by the voice of teaching. Their hearts and their eyes with their ears were closed, because the doors of their thoughts were shut by their own will. When the measure of the sins of the wicked overflowed, and the opportunity of repentance was lessened and diminished, when the whole generation was corrupted by cutting off hope and by wrath, He shut the door of mercies and confined them. When the Avenger waited and tarried that they might ask of Him, and no voice was found pleading to obtain forgiveness, then grace was ashamed before justice: How long will You be longsuffering, since they have gained no benefit?
When the stories of that ark were built, nothing remained but that Noah should enter, and then wrath would come.

entries.section: 1. The ship or the wooden idol?

paragraphs.text: St. Jacob of Serugh For blessed is the wood by which righteousness comes. [7]

God used the wood of the ark to rescue His believers, instead of the wooden idols that sailors suppose able to rescue them from the dangers of the seas, whether the raging waves or the pirates of the seas.

Here he compares the wooden idol with the wood of the Cross. The first is an idol that falls under the curse, with its maker and the one who worships it. But the second bore the Savior of the whole world.

* The Lord of Abraham came to the house of His friends to visit them, and when the sons of Abraham went out they gave Him the Cross. He was carrying His Cross, and going out from the one who crucified Him, her Lord, because she gave Him in return for His kindnesses nothing but this (the Cross). He became a physician to her and healed all her wounds, and when He went out He took no provision but the Cross. The sentence of iniquity was passed on the Son of God, and He went out to die with the wicked without guilt (Mk 15:28).
St. Jacob of Serugh * The Gospel says: “And they took Jesus, and led Him away. And He bearing His cross went forth into a place called the place of a skull” (Jn 19:16-17).
Jesus went forth to the place where He was to be crucified, bearing His Cross...
What a great sight!
The wicked beholder sees it as a sight full of mockery, but the godly beholder sees it as a great mystery!
The wicked sees in it a great confirmation of disgrace and shame, and the godly sees it as an impregnable fortress of faith!

The wicked sees it and laughs, seeing a King carrying the tree of punishment instead of the scepter of kingship, but the godly sees a King carrying the Cross for his own crucifixion... where the Cross will be set upon the foreheads... as the Apostle Paul says: “But God forbid that I should glory, save in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Gal 6:14).
He was praising the very Cross of Christ, which He bore upon His shoulders, as a shining lamp burning without being put under a bushel (Mt 5:15).
St. Augustine * By the tree by which (Satan) killed us, the Lord rescued us!
By the wine by which we became crazed, we became (in Communion) pure!
From the (divine) side a secret power flowed, which shattered Satan like Dagon (1 Sam 5:1-5), for in this ark is hidden a book that cries out for us: “The Conqueror” (the Lord Christ)!
Blessed is He who as a true Lamb saved us, and destroyed our destroyer as happened with Dagon!

The old wolf (Satan) saw the Lamb... and was terrified of Him though he hid himself. For as the wolf put on the garment of lambs, so the Shepherd became a “Lamb” among the lambs, so that when the greedy wolf dared to devour the gentle Lamb, this Almighty One would repel that devourer!

entries.section: 1. The ship or the wooden idol?

paragraphs.text: St. Ephrem the Syrian But that which is made an idol is cursed, both it and he that made it: he, because he made it; and it, because, being corruptible, it was called god. [8]

The wise man offers the mystery of the curse of both the material of the idol and its maker. The material in itself is not evil, nor is man as God's creature evil, for all that God created is good. The evil of the material lies in its use as an idol, which usurps the glory of God and which the devil inhabits to deceive men by it. And the evil of man is not in his body nor in his soul, but in the perversion of his will, in which he bears a will that resists the divine truth.
The world is beautiful and good, and the body is good and the soul is good; the deviation of any creature from the course for which it was created corrupts its being and makes it evil.

* “But that which is made an idol is cursed, both it and he that made it” (Wis 14:8) does not mean that what has no life in it is cursed in itself, but by the word “made” he means precisely the lifeless idol (in which Satan dwells).

entries.section: 1. The ship or the wooden idol?

paragraphs.text: Origen For God hates the ungodly and his ungodliness alike. [9]

God does not hate His creation, but He cannot bear what is not in harmony with His holiness. The wicked man who denies the faith, whether by his mouth or by his work, cannot enjoy fellowship with the Holy One unless he accepts sanctification by the Spirit of God.
Here God hates the evil will of the wicked man, as He hates evil itself.

entries.section: 1. The ship or the wooden idol?

paragraphs.text: So the thing made and the maker are punished. [10]

Often God allowed the prophets to destroy idols, as Moses the prophet did, who ground the golden calf to powder and scattered it (Ex 32:20). As for idolaters, God allows them to be disciplined in this world, and if they do not cease, their punishment will be the eternal fire of Gehenna.

entries.section: 1. The ship or the wooden idol?

paragraphs.text: Therefore there shall be a visitation also upon the idols of the Gentiles, because they have become an abomination in God's creation, and a stumbling block to the souls of men, and a snare to the feet of the foolish. [11]
Sadly, Solomon the wise himself, when he married foreign pagan women, worshipped their gods (1 Kgs 11:8); how much more are simple souls exposed to fall into this worship!

entries.section: 2. Fornication behind idolatry

paragraphs.text: 12 For the devising of idols was the beginning of fornication, and the invention of them the corruption of life. 13 For they were not from the beginning, neither shall they be for ever. The idea of making idols is the origin of fornication, and the invention of them is the corruption of life. [12]

Man was created bearing within himself a natural law that urges him to worship the living God, and he finds rest and peace in fulfilling this impulse; but when man turned his back to God and rejected His divine commandment, the lusts of his body rose against him and took possession of and ruled over his will. At the same time he wants to worship, so he exchanged the invisible God, who rebukes his conscience, for false gods that he sees and touches and appeases by every means, even by wounding his body or slaughtering his children, to quiet his conscience.

Idol worship is bound up with fornication. For on one side the relation of believers with God is like the relation of a bride with her bridegroom, so that if she turns her back to Him to be joined to pagan gods she has fallen into marital unfaithfulness. Therefore it was said of unfaithful Israel: “Where is the bill of your mother's divorcement?” (Isa 50:1). It was also said: “Take heed to yourself, lest you make a covenant with the inhabitants of the land, and they go a whoring after their gods, and do sacrifice unto their gods, and one call you, and you eat of his sacrifice; and you take of their daughters unto your sons, and their daughters go a whoring after their gods, and make your sons go a whoring after their gods” (Ex 34:15-16). The origin of idolatry is the corruption of man's thought and unfaithfulness to God the Creator, which is counted as fornication of the soul that abandons its union with its Creator to be joined to accursed idols.
On the other hand, idolatry has often been bound up with bodily fornication, sometimes even in the temples of the idols themselves.

The connection of idolatry with fornication appears from what is recorded of the people's worship of the golden calf, for it was said: “the people sat down to eat and to drink, and rose up to play” (Ex 32:6). Here “play” means sexual caresses.
* (Idol worship) was discovered among men for no reason other than the existence of passions among those who imagined it.

* When the human soul had experienced various pleasures, and forgot divine things, and was the more delighted with the pleasures of the body that it set before its eyes, and cared for nothing but present things and contemplating them, it no longer thought that there is any good except temporal and bodily things. Therefore, having turned aside and forgotten that it was in the image of the good God, it no longer had the power by which it saw God the Word, after whose likeness it was created. But having withdrawn from itself, it began to imagine and fancy what has no existence.

* When the men of the former age lost their minds, and sank in passions and the fancies of bodily things, and forgot the knowledge of God and His glory because of the dullness of their minds, or rather the absence of their minds, they made for themselves gods of visible things, glorifying the creature rather than the Creator God, and deifying the things made rather than the Lord, their cause and Creator.
Pope Athanasius the Apostolic * He who serves vain gods is without doubt an adulterer away from the truth, for all vanity is fornication. Thus he sinks into fornication.

Tertullian * Blessed is Rachel, who hid the idols of the vain Gentiles and declared that their images were full of uncleanness. And let no one think that she offended against the honor of her father and her reverence for him as a father, because she sat while he stood (Gen 31:35). For it is written: “He that loves father or mother more than Me is not worthy of Me” (Mt 10:37).

The woman who commits adultery does not cleave to her husband, and is not one flesh with him (1 Cor 6:15-16), but isolates herself and separates herself from him by her adultery. So every soul that does not cleave to God but walks in fornication by submitting to the worship of vain idols is separated from the Lord by the grievous defilement of holy things, when it ought to have cleaved to Him. And he who withdraws from the Lord perishes.
St. Ambrose

entries.section: 2. Fornication behind idolatry

paragraphs.text: They were not in the beginning, neither shall they be for ever. [13]

When man was created good and pure, purity was bound up with the worship of God the Creator from the beginning. But when corruption gained mastery over man, and he enslaved himself to bodily pleasures and fell into fornication, he turned aside from worshipping the Holy One and began to worship idols or creatures, and these will pass away one day.
Cleaving to the true, holy God brings us into immortality, where divine righteousness is, while indulgence in bodily lusts drives us to perdition and destruction, because they do not last.

entries.section: 3. Vainglory and idolatry

paragraphs.text: 14 For by the vain glory of men they entered into the world, and therefore shall they come shortly to an end.
They entered the world through men's love of vainglory, and therefore a speedy end was written for them. [14]

Besides fornication there is another motive for idol worship, namely the love of vainglory. For the worship of the humble God moves the soul to enjoy inner glory, but the worship of vain idols glorifies man and his handiwork.

It is as though the worship of the humble Holy One is bound up with humble souls, and the worship of idols and enslavement to the proud Satan is bound up with man's fall. We do not wonder at the warning of Holy Scripture: “God resists the proud.”

entries.section: 4. Immortalizing the dead and idolatry

paragraphs.text: 15 For a father afflicted with untimely mourning, when he has made an image of his child who was suddenly taken away, now honored him as a god, who was then a dead man, and delivered to those that were under him ceremonies and sacrifices. 16 Thus in process of time an ungodly custom, grown strong, was kept as a law, and graven images were worshipped by the commandments of kings. 17 Whom men could not honor in presence, because they dwelt far off, they took the counterfeit of his visage from afar, and made an express image of a king whom they honored, to flatter the absent as if he were present.

There is a father afflicted with untimely mourning, who made an image of his son who was suddenly taken away, and began to honor with the honor of a god him who yesterday was a dead man, and ordained for those under his hand mysteries and rites. [15]

The author gives an example of the origin of idol worship. A father who lost his young son made a statue for him as a memorial, and the remembrance turned into worship, and he devised for himself a particular system for worshipping the statue of his son.
It is natural that children and grandchildren should worship their ancestors (2 Macc 11:13), but the worship of dead children was also known among the Egyptians and others.
It is reported of Cicero the famous orator that he deified his daughter Tullia after her death.

entries.section: 4. Immortalizing the dead and idolatry

paragraphs.text: Then this wicked custom became firmly established with the passing of time, and was kept as a law, and by the commands of kings the carved images became objects of worship. [16]
The second example of the origin of idolatry is the kings' setting up statues to honor themselves, and then demanding that the people worship them.
The deification of rulers was spread by Euhemerus about 290 B.C.

entries.section: The worship of emperors

paragraphs.text: And men who could not honor them in their presence, because of the distance of their dwelling, portrayed their likeness from afar, and made a visible image of the king whom they honored, that by their zeal they might express flattery to the absent as though present. [17]

Among the chief evils of idol worship is the instilling of the spirit of hypocrisy, for the great and the people vied with one another to offer worship to the statues of kings out of flattery and adulation, regarding his statue as standing in his place.
* Let us reckon that all idol worship is worship offered to men...

Idol worship is condemned not because of the persons who are the object of worship, but because of its being practiced on behalf of demons. “Render therefore unto Caesar the things which are Caesar's” (Mt 22:21; Mk 12:17; Lk 20:25).

It is enough to set against this: “Render unto God the things that are God's.” What then remains for Caesar...? The Lord asked that they bring Him money, and asked whose image is this? And when He heard that it was Caesar's, He said: “Render therefore unto Caesar the things which are Caesar's.”
* We pray to the eternal God, the true God, the living God, for the health of our rulers...

It is fitting for them to realize from whom they received their authority, that as men they know from whom they received life itself. They are convinced that He is the only God, and on His power they depend entirely...

To Him we Christians lift up our eyes and spread out our hands, being innocent, and with our heads uncovered because we have no need to be ashamed, and finally without anyone to prompt us, because we pray from the heart, and pray constantly for all our emperors. We ask for them a long life, a peaceful empire, a safe dwelling, strong armies, a faithful senate, a world at peace, and everything that this man and Caesar desire.
* We honor the Emperor as we are permitted to honor him, as a man who comes after God.
Tertullian

entries.section: 5. Flattery behind idolatry

paragraphs.text: 18 Also the singular diligence of the artificer helped to set forward the ignorant to more superstition. 19 For he, perhaps willing to please one in authority, labored with all his skill to make the likeness of the best fashion. 20 And so the multitude, allured by the grace of the work, took him now for a god, who a little before was but honored as a man. 21 And this was an occasion to deceive the world: for men, serving either calamity or tyranny, ascribed unto stones and stocks the incommunicable Name.
Then the ambition of the artist impelled even those who did not know him to spread his worship. [18]

Misuse of gifts: the artist who makes statues does not make them for kings as they are, but they labor to pour upon them a touch of beauty that is not found in the kings themselves. So art was turned into a snare to catch men into evil.

entries.section: 5. Flattery behind idolatry

paragraphs.text: And perhaps he wished to please the king, so he strained his art that the result might be more beautiful than the reality. [19]
With the skill with which the artist was endowed, what occupies him is not respect for his artistic gift but pleasing the king, for material or moral gain.

entries.section: 5. Flattery behind idolatry

paragraphs.text: So the crowd, allured by the splendor of his work, took for a god him whom a little before they honored as a man. [20]

The artist misused his gift, and offered his art to entice men to attribute divinity to a man. And God Himself warned us of this, saying: “I am the Lord: that is My name: and My glory will I not give to another, neither My praise to graven images” (Isa 42:8).

entries.section: 5. Flattery behind idolatry

paragraphs.text: And this became a hidden snare for mankind, that men enslaved by calamity or royal authority gave to stones and wood the incommunicable Name. [21]

The wise man counts the setting up of idols and the worship of them as a catastrophe, whose motive is often the love of power and temporal glory, so that emperors and the great set up their statues as objects of worship, to which the people give what is fitting for God alone.

entries.section: 6. Idolatry and deception

paragraphs.text: 22 Afterward it was not enough for them that they erred in the knowledge of God, but they live in the great war of ignorance, and those so great plagues they call peace. 23 For while they slay their children in sacrifices, or use secret ceremonies, or make revels of strange rites; 24 they keep neither lives nor marriages any longer pure, but one slays another traitorously, or grieves him by adultery. 25 So that there reigns in all men without exception blood, manslaughter, theft and dissimulation, corruption, unfaithfulness, tumults, perjury, 26 disquieting of good men, forgetfulness of good turns, defiling of souls, changing of kind, disorder in marriages, adultery and shameless uncleanness. 27 For the worship of idols not to be named is the beginning, the cause, and the end of all evil. 28 For either they are mad when they are merry, or prophesy lies, or live unjustly, or lightly forswear themselves. 29 For insomuch as their trust is in idols, which have no life, though they swear falsely, yet they look not to be hurt.

After setting forth the motives for the worship of idols, namely fornication and the love of vainglory, the immortalizing of the dead and flattery of emperors and the great, he tells us of the role of idol worship in deceiving men.

entries.section: a. Error of knowledge

paragraphs.text: Then it was not enough for them to err in the knowledge of God, but they plunged into the wide war of ignorance, and called such evils peace. [22]

If pagan worship puts weak creatures and lifeless, dead idols in the place of God, and offers them the worship and glorification fitting for God alone, what is more serious than this is that in doing so they deceive themselves, claiming to be in deep inner peace. For more serious than ignorance is that a man should suppose in his ignorance that he has wisdom, and in his deprivation of inner peace that he is possessed of peace.

Perhaps he means here that idol worshippers used to hold feasts and practice evils and abominations under the cover of joy and peace. The wicked look upon the children of God as though they were devoid of life, joy and peace. And they pretend to grieve for the believers because they are deprived of happiness.
The wicked theological thought of the pagans drives them to a life of licentious amusement.
* Christ is our peace (Rom 5:1). Therefore the way of peace is the way of Christ, which the wicked do not know.
Origen

entries.section: b. Insane customs

paragraphs.text: We saw the wise man looking with bitterness at idol worshippers because they were ignorant of the true knowledge of God, and in this ignorance they suppose that they enjoy happiness and peace. Now he adds a third factor, namely their performing shameful practices and rites unbecoming to them as men.
And with their rites that kill children, and their hidden mysteries, or their insane festivals with strange customs. [23]

By the word “rites” he means “ceremonies”; instead of the ceremony being an order fitting for man in God's holy creation, killing became among their important ceremonies, under the cover of offering sacrifices to the gods. Fathers lost their fatherhood and mothers their motherhood, and they agreed together to offer children as sacrifices to the pagan gods.
And if they were asked what lies behind this brutal act, they answered: It is a hidden mystery that none can understand.
Besides this brutal violence they practice strange customs on the days of their festivals, which often means perverse bodily practices.

Pope Athanasius the Apostolic gives us horrible examples of human sacrifices, of which we mention: 1. Some used to offer men as sacrifices to idols bearing the image of dead men, offering living creatures as sacrifices to dead creatures, and rational beings to motionless things. 2. The Taurians, a division of the Scythians, who lived in the Crimean peninsula in southern Russia. They used to seize those who had escaped from wrecked ships and offer them as sacrifices to their virgin, as they call her. So in cruelty and brutality they show that those whom their gods saved from drowning are slaughtered. 3. Some of the Scythians used to divide the spoils of war into groups, each group comprising a hundred men, and they chose one from each group and slaughtered him as an offering to their gods. 4. The ancient Egyptians used to offer human sacrifices to Hera. The Cretans and Phoenicians used to appease the face of Cronos by slaughtering their children. Even the ancient Romans used to offer human sacrifices in their worship of Jupiter Latius, the god who was regarded as protector of the Italian league composed of thirty Latin cities.

entries.section: b. Insane customs

paragraphs.text: They no longer keep purity in life, nor in marriage, but one kills another, or grieves him by adultery. [24]

When they deprive themselves of fellowship with the Holy One, they are joined to Satan, who cannot bear chastity and holiness, but wants every man to fall into defilement, even in marriage, practicing perverse and unseemly things.

Their rule becomes pleasure whatever the cost, so there is nothing to prevent a man from killing another to seize his wife or daughter. He may even rape her before his eyes, threatening him with death, and this is what he means by “grieves him by adultery.”

entries.section: b. Insane customs

paragraphs.text: Evil abounds, for there is blood and killing and theft and deceit and corruption and unfaithfulness and tumult and false witness. [25]

When man leaves the worship of the living God, his life turns into a chain of evils that does not stop, “evil abounds.” He cares nothing for the shedding of blood, or killing, or theft, or deceit, or corruption, or unfaithfulness, or tumult, or false witness.

entries.section: b. Insane customs

paragraphs.text: And confusion of values and ingratitude for grace, and defiling of souls, and sexual perversion, and disorder in marriage, and adultery and licentiousness. [26]
They live without any regard for human or social values, with denial of divine grace, and defilement of soul and body, and licentiousness, and so on.
Idol worshippers suppose that as free men it is their right to practice evils and perversions in unrestrained wantonness. They are rights that no one may deprive them of.

* Rachel, that is the Church or discernment, hid the idols (Gen 31:34), for the Church does not know statues and forms of idols in which there is nothing of the truth, but knows the true existence of the Trinity. Truly she destroys the darkness and declares the radiance of glory. Let us then forsake the darkness and seek the sun. Let us leave the smoke and strive for the light. Smoke is evil; for as smoke is to the eyes (Prov 10:26), so is evil to those who practice it.

entries.section: b. Insane customs

paragraphs.text: St. Ambrose For the worship of nameless idols is the beginning, the cause and the end of all evil. [27]

The wise man sees that idol worship does not deserve to have a name, because it rejects the name of the Holy One, and that it is the source of all evil, and behind all corruption and dissolution and license, and indeed it is the goal of evil, in which man denies his Creator and worships the wicked enemy in one form or another.

entries.section: c. Rejoicing in evil

paragraphs.text: For those who worship them rejoice to madness, or prophesy lies, or live in injustice, or lightly bear false witness. [28]

After speaking of the effect of idol worship, from the lulling of the conscience to the rejection of fellowship with the holy God, and the practice of every sort of evils, he makes clear that the wicked cover evil with an atmosphere of joy, but it is not the calm inner joy, but “they rejoice to madness”; they claim prophecy, helped in this by the devil the liar, and they walk in a spirit of injustice and false witness. This was characteristic of the priests of the idols in particular.

* The father (Jacob) was commanded to dwell there in Bethel, and there he was commanded to make an altar to God who appeared to him (Gen 35:1). There he took the strange gods and buried them under the terebinth (Gen 35:4) in Jerusalem. There also Rachel was buried on the way to Ephrath, that is Bethlehem (Gen 35:19), and there Jacob set a pillar upon her grave (Gen 35:20). What great mysteries! There is the Church of God, where God appeared and spoke with His humble servants.
